Vision Accessibility is a project focused on improving visual accessibility in FreeBSD by documenting, developing, and integrating assistive technologies for blind and visually impaired users.

During this quarter, work focused mainly on Milestone 2: creating new accessible themes for TUI utilities in the FreeBSD base system, with the ability to select one during the OS installation.

The next version of bsddialog was developed as part of this work, with a focus on improving its theming support. The theming code was reorganized and improved, and the bsddialog_theme.h API was extended to allow applications to select and customize themes more easily and automatically.

In particular, the library initialization process now uses bsddialog_get_auto_theme(), which automatically detects the theme to use. If available, the theme can be selected through a centralized system-wide or user-specific configuration file. This allows utilities in the FreeBSD base system, such as tzsetup(8) and bsdinstall(8), as well as ports such as ports-mgmt/portconfig, to use the same theme configuration without requiring individual changes to each application.

Several accessibility-oriented themes were also improved or added:

Improved the built-in black-and-white theme. It was originally designed for terminals without color support, but it is also useful for presenting information without relying on colors alone.

Added a theme without red, using black, blue, cyan, white, and yellow.

Added a theme without yellow and blue, using black, green, red, and white.

Added a new high-contrast theme, using black, magenta, white, and yellow.

The new functionality has been documented in the manual pages, with new examples, and in the bsddialog CHANGELOG.

The design and implementation phases have been completed, and testing is now starting. The new functionality is currently available only in the main branch of the bsddialog repository.

The next steps are to complete testing, release version 1.2, update the devel/bsddialog port, and import the new version into FreeBSD BASE.

During this quarter, a HumanWare BrailleNote Apex was acquired for use in the upcoming milestones. A suitable charger was received and the device was successfully tested. The Braille display and keyboard are working, as is the built-in speech synthesizer.

Although the Braille subsystem is planned for a future milestone, initial experimentation has already started because designing and integrating such a subsystem is a complex task. These first tests are intended to provide practical information for its future design and implementation.

The BrailleNote Apex is not simply a Braille display, but a Braille notetaker running Windows Embedded CE 6.0. It provides a one-dimensional user interface through KeySoft, with applications such as a word processor, email, web browsing, and other functionality. The Apex was also connected to an external monitor through VGA, which made it easier to explore and better understand its functionality.

Using the Apex requires familiarity with Braille, both for writing through the Braille keyboard and for reading through the Braille display. For this reason, LearnBraille was also developed and used. It is a simple Lua script that uses devel/liblouis to provide a quiz for practicing Braille characters.

The Apex was connected to FreeBSD through USB and used in its "Screen Reader Terminal" mode, which allows the device to operate as a Braille display connected to another computer. The device is recognized by uipaq(4), and communication is provided through the man:ucom interface[4]. This is consistent with the deviceâs architecture, as the Apex runs Windows Embedded CE 6.0.

Initial communication tests were successful in both directions. Data was sent from FreeBSD to the Braille display, including a simple "Hello World, FreeBSD!" message rendered on the Braille cells. Characters typed on the Braille keyboard were also received by FreeBSD. In this direction, each Braille character is represented by one byte, with its bits corresponding to the Braille dots.

Further tests, documentation, and information about the progress and results of this work will be provided in future reports.

Links: x11appjail on GitHub URL: https://github.com/DtxdF/x11appjail Contact: JesÃºs Daniel Colmenares Oviedo

x11appjail is a specialized tool for creating, verifying, installing, and running AppJails. An AppJail is a CLI, TUI or X11 application that runs inside a FreeBSD jail but is perceived by the end user as identical (or at least very similar) to an application running directly on the host system.

This tool makes extensive use of appjail(1) as its engine; however, unlike the latter, the primary user in x11appjail is neither root nor a privileged user, but rather an unprivileged user. The fundamental goal of this project is to grant the user limited access to the jail, restricted solely to the execution of a CLI, TUI or X11 application.

This project began months ago as a prototype to establish a workflow leveraging appjail-x11(1); however, starting with version 1.0.0, it was rewritten from scratch into a unified tool that integrates all its projects, such as sysutils/appjail, sysutils/unixexec, archivers/appscript, and sysutils/jtransfer, among others. Even better, it allows for the execution of not only X11 applications but also CLI and TUI programs.

The most relevant project for x11appjail(1) is not only appjail(1), but also appscript(1). My goal with appscript(1) is to create an ultra-lightweight alternative to AppImage for FreeBSD that does not depend on FUSE, thus eliminating the need to configure vfs.usermount=1. appscript(1) allows you to create an elf(5) executable that contains everything necessary to run a self-contained executable.

The most significant changes and improvements for appscript(1) and x11appjail(1) are:

Executables created by appscript(1) extract the payload cooperatively: the leader process extracts the payload once using an exclusive lock, while other processes (if any) wait using a shared lock. Unlike previous versions, where the payload was extracted to a random directory upon every execution, this significantly improves performance by extracting the payload only once; furthermore, the resulting directory is removed by the last remaining process once no running processes remain.

appscript-verify(1) is a new command installed by archivers/appscript to verify executables signed with signify(1); it is particularly relevant to x11appjail(1)'s veriexec (see below).

x11appjail(1)'s veriexec is an internal tool used by x11appjail(1) to run an AppJail in portable mode only if it is signed with a trusted key. This tool is unrelated to NetBSDâs veriexec.

Both tools support the classic, battle-tested SHA-256 algorithm and the faster yet secure BLAKE3 algorithm. When sysutils/b3sum is available (the default if x11appjail(1) was installed from ports), BLAKE3 is the default choice, unless SHA-256 is explicitly specified in rc.conf(5).

The checksum algorithm is fundamental to both x11appjail(1) and appscript(1). In the case of x11appjail(1), the algorithm is used in internal operations such as veriexec, whereas appscript(1) uses it to verify executables. BLAKE3 has been selected as the default option because it offers greater speed without compromising security.

Attributes have been implemented in x11appjail(1) as a means for both the user and the system operator to manipulate the behavior of an AppJail. For example, a system operator can create the system attribute users.uid.perms, the content of which might be "enable_3d sound usb webcam". An unprivileged user can create the user attributes appname:profile.allow.enable_3d and appname:profile.allow.sound. Subsequently, when executing an AppJail, devices become visible or remain hidden depending on whether the user holds the corresponding permission and has authorized those permissions for the jail being created. In this case, the hardware acceleration and sound devices will become visible, provided the AppJail has incorporated the necessary logic to make them visible.

Another notable change worth mentioning for x11appjail(1) are the examples added in ${EXAMPLESDIR}/Apps: badwolf, chromium, evince, feh, firefox, htop, linux-brave, mpv, nanonote, telegram-desktop and thunderbird. Beyond the applications themselves, the key factor is the deployment method. htop is an example of a CLI application, linux-brave is a Linux application, and the others are X11 applications. Web browsers, Mpv, and Thunderbird are the most interesting examples, as they demonstrate how an AppJail can use VirtualGL to properly enable hardware acceleration within a FreeBSD jail, something that would not normally be possible given that Xephyr is the backend used by appjail-x11(1). Best of all, from the end-userâs perspective, all of this is transparent.

Links: link: The commit series of the port URL: https://github.com/linux-rdma/rdma-core/pull/1778 link: LinuxAPI project URL: https://github.com/freebsd/linuxapi

Contact: Konstantin Belousov Contact: Ariel Ehrenberg Contact: Slava Shwartsman Contact: Gleb Popov

The Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) infrastructure provides high-performance interconnect between computing and storage nodes. It can operate over different physical networks, for instance Ethernet and Infiniband.

The implementation of the RDMA stack consists of several components. There is the core kernel infrastructure, and drivers for Host Channel Adapters (HCAs), providing access to the kernel verbs. Userspace applications never interact with the kernel devices directly, the core libibverbs library and vendor-specific userspace drivers provide unified and device-specific verbs.

Since RDMA intent of providing low-latency low-overhead operations, performant HCAs offload a lot of operations from CPU. Also, typical in-line operations like send and receive can be initiated and completed in userspace, where kernel only assists in the connection establishment and teardown. Due to this, the userspace RDMA software stack is crucial for its operations.

FreeBSD base system includes port of the so called OFED kernel core component, kernel drivers, as well as userspace core (libibverbs) and userspace drivers, for instance libmlx5 for managing Nvidia Connect-X4 and later HCAs. Over time, the kernel parts get some significant updates from the infiniband code in the Linux kernel, which become the home for updated OFED. Userspace part of OFED was converted into the rdma-core userspace project, that only supports Linux (and glibc). Since userspace drivers in rdma-core provide essential functionality, and since FreeBSD userspace RDMA components are quite outdated, the situation overall needs a resolution.

We attempted to update the in-tree userspace components by importing the series of rdma-core commits with dependencies, but it quickly proved to be not feasible. Instead we started looking at what it would take to make rdma-core compile and run on FreeBSD.

First, there were a number of missing glibc-specific APIs that were used in rdma-core, for instance, strdupa() and friends, main:tdestroy(3), some pthread functions. These were easy to handle in the base system, and addition of them benefited the whole FreeBSD porting story.

Next, and more serious, the unportable features of glibc were used everywhere in the sources, and trying to cover them all would cause huge porting patch, which is problematic to push upstream, even for cooperating upstream. Instead, the idea of using an approach similar to LinuxKPI for kernel code, was formed and developed, called LinuxAPI. Unlike LinuxKPI, which handles architectural mismatches between Linux kernel and FreeBSD kernel, in addition to the different C interfaces, LinuxAPI needs to smooth out the differences around extensions to the same core functionality defined by POSIX. It is mostly about bits that are not defined by POSIX but needed for RDMA to function, like networking interface enumeration, or discovery of the rdma-capable devices and their capabilities etc.

It seems that people consider the LinuxAPI useful outside the rdma-core porting efforts already, there is a project github.com/freebsd/linuxapi which takes the developed set of headers and extends it further. We are currently working on providing the permissive license to make the library useful without additional strings attached.

Our initial goal, also limited by the available hardware, is to have rdma-core work with the ConnectX-4 cards. Of course we welcome all vendors interested in RDMA on FreeBSD to improve the port to properly support their cards.

The result of the porting is available as the repository. Also we try to upstream the changes so that FreeBSD would become the second natively supported platform for rdma-core. The Pull Request to the github project is submitted. There is currently a blocking discussion about the way to organize CI for FreeBSD platform. Gleb Popov created the net/rdma-core port from the forked sources, which is already in the ports tree.

The kernel changes to get the port working were surprisingly small and contained. They mostly consisted of bug fixes for the code paths not previously exercised by userspace since there were no userspace. Most interesting part was perhaps the difference in ioctl(2) behavior between Linux and FreeBSD, where Linux can both return an error and copyout the data structure. The issue was already observed in the LinuxKPI, and the porting work provided the generic solution there.

Links: Up-to-date NFS server sources in branch freebsd-rdma URL: https://github.com/viniciusferrao/freebsd-src.git nfs-over-rdma-setup.txt URL: https://people.freebsd.org/~rmacklem/nfs-over-rdma-setup.txt

Contact: Rick Macklem , Vinicius Ferrao

Currently FreeBSDâs NFS is supported over TCP (and UDP for NFSv3). This project adds support for NFS over RDMA, as described by RFC-8166 and RFC-8267. This should allow RDMA aware NICs to offload most of the network transport and improve performance over fast LAN fabrics.

Thanks to Vinicius, a lot of progress has been made. He has the NFS server side working, and quite well from what I know.

The client side is now testing quite well against Viniciusâs server and both client and server are now ready for third party testing. To test, a client and server with Mellanox ConnectX4â6 NICs running a kernel built from recent FreeBSD main sources is needed.

See nfs-over-rdma-setup.txt for information on setting up a testing environment.

A stable/15 kernel should be sufficient for the loadable modules in a few weeks. The client code should also be committed to FreeBSDâs main in a few weeks, with an MFC to stable/15 be the end of 2026. The server code was created via generative AI and the FreeBSD project is working on a policy for handling generative AI submissions. In the meantime, the server code will be available as an "unofficial port" that builds a kernel loadable module.

Third party testing would be appreciated.

Thanks go to Vinicius for the NFS server work and to the FreeBSD Netperf cluster folk, without which I would have never gotten this code tested.

Links: D59438 URL: https://reviews.freebsd.org/D59438 rG60c7313074b9 URL: https://cgit.freebsd.org/src/commit/?id=60c7313074b93adf4ea70ff44b78b3b4fc15c29f

Contact: Devin Teske

nfsstat(1) reports the server as a whole. nfsdtop(8) reports the user, the group, or the client behind the reads and writes. It is a top-like display, taken with dtrace(1) from the nfsd(8) paths nfsrvd_read, nfsvno_read, nfsrvd_write, and nfsvno_write.

The default view is per user. -g coalesces by group, and -c by IPv4 client. Each interval prints a total, then the rows that did the I/O, sorted by combined read and write volume. The default interval is two seconds. The columns are humanized bandwidth unless -b asks for the bytes moved in that interval. WRITE(IN) is data the clients sent. READ(OUT) is data the server sent.

A UID, GID, or client address on those paths belongs to the client, not to the server. nfsdtop(8) does not ask getent(1) to name them while it samples. Names come from map files in the current directory: .nfsd.passwd, .nfsd.group, and .nfsd.hosts. A filter (-U, -G, or -C) is resolved once, from those maps and then with getent(1) or host(1), and the result is compiled into the dtrace(1) predicate.

-j emits one JSON object for the view total and one per key, each interval, with the byte counts and the rates. -J samples the client, group, and user views together:

Only root, or a user who can run dtrace(1), can run it. The client view and -C are IPv4 only. -R, or a non-empty NFSDTOP_REDACT, replaces names that are not well-known system accounts with random strings of the same length.

The introduction is in HEAD as of 60c7313074b9 (D59438), and nfsdtop(8) makes its first release in FreeBSD 16.0.

Thanks to Alexander Ziaee and Benedict Reuschling for the man page, to Adrian Chadd for review, and to Rick Macklem for a look at the NFS side.

Run it on a server that is already busy. If the row you need is not a user, a group, or a client, please write.

Links: GSoC project Wiki page URL: https://wiki.freebsd.org/SummerOfCode2026Projects/EnhancingZonedStorageSupportOnFreeBSD

Work on this project intends to enhance Zoned Storage support in FreeBSD, by adding the following new features:

New gzoned(8) GEOM driver for emulating zoned devices.

Zoned Namespaces (ZNS) support for zoned NVMe drives.

Improved Zoned Storage handling for gconcat(8), glabel(8), and gpart(8).

The work was carried out as part of Google Summer of Code 2026.

The new gzoned(8) driver emulates Zoned Storage on top of regular, non-zoned drives, allowing for development, testing, and integration of Zoned Storage without zoned hardware.

ZNS support enables using Zoned Storage on NVMe SSDs.

Zone-aware GEOM classes let host-managed drives be used with the usual storage tools.

ZNS support was added to the nda(4) driver, while nvd(4) support is not planned due to its barebones nature.

Host-managed devices can now be concatenated through gconcat(8), while glabel(8) will cleanly refuse them for automatic labeling due to its metadata requirement. gpart(8) can now create GPT partition schemes on host-managed drives by not writing the backup GPT table.

Polish up gconcat(8), glabel(8), and ZNS support, as they can now rely on gzoned(8) from main.

Mentors: Robert Clausecker, Alan Somers, and Ken Merry Sponsor: Google Summer of Code 2026

I was off for university from May to August and I am back to working on this now. Since I could not accomplish this task for LLVM 23, the target release for completion has changed to LLVM 24.

armv7 and powerpc64be are support candidates now. Once LLDB refactoring is done, I will implement support for those architectures.

Unlike KGDB that uses custom frame sniffer for trapframe unwinding, LLDB uses DWARF CFI instead. DWARF CFI works on KGDB as well; when a frame is not recognized by KGDBâs frame sniffer, it will fall back to CFI. Thus, no change on the KGDB side is needed.

Contact: Konstantin Belousov

The process descriptors API enhancements project continued, with the goal to allow complete process control using descriptors, in particular, debugging. I wanted to make it possible to stop reference pids as the process identifiers. The milestone for it should be a demonstration of enabling the capsicum mode for some non-trivial debugger, I selected truss(1) because it does not need neither filesystem nor network namespace accesses after attached to the target.

The semi-obvious solution there is to introduce pdptrace(2), which is equivalent to ptrace(2) but takes the process descriptor as the process designator. We need to be able to obtain the notifications of the process debugging events, which are provided by waitpid[2] syscall family for pid-based controls. And, we need a way to obtain the process descriptor for a new child forked from the debuggee, to continue tracing of all descendants.

Previously, the pdopenpid(2) system call was added, which allows to get a handle on an arbitrary process. Existing operations on the process descriptors are somewhat limited: handle owner can wait for the exit notification using kqueue(2), and with some luck retrieve the process exit status.

The last point requires some elaboration. Since the pdwait(2) call was added recently, there were some amount of hacks in the kernel to allow waitpid(2) calls on pidâs of processes created with pdfork(2). As result, the waitpid(2) caller might have reaped the process before owner of the process descriptor could call pdwait(2). Similarly, if there is more than one process descriptor opened on the same process, only the first pdwait(2) caller could retrieve the exit status with pdwait(2), making other descriptors useless.

The listed set of problems also made it very hard to correctly use the proposed pdptrace(2). The process being debugged could steal events from process descriptors and vice versa. Simply disallowing wait(2) on processes with the opened descriptors is not an option for two reasons: * backward compatibility, waitpid(2) was already allowed and existing binaries relied on it * if the debuggee used fork(2) to create a child, it expects to get the exit notification (e.g. SIGCHLD) and exit status from wait(2)

The solution was manyfold. First, we have to postpone reaping if there are either opened process descriptors, or if the process was created with fork(2), we should not reap until wait(2) is called on pid by the parent. Second, the exit status needs to be preserved in the process descriptors private data even after reaping, to allow pdwait(2) on any of the descriptors. This was implemented by providing a bitmap of the 'zombie refs' on the kernel struct proc. Each zombie reference prevents reaping, and cleared by corresponding call to waitpid(2) or pdwait(2). Only when all registered references are cleared, zombie can be reaped. If the process is created with pdfork(2) or opened with pdopenpid[2], it gets the procdesc zombie reference. If the process was created with fork(2), it gets the 'parent' zombie reference. By default, pdfork[2] also sets the parent reference to allow the waitpid(2), for compatibility. The new pdfork(2) flag PD_NOWAITPID prevents that.

Then, wait-like events must work with the process descriptors. The procdesc kqueue(2) event filter was extended with NOTE_PDSIGCHLD hints to report that pdwait(2) can retrieve tracing or exiting event on the descriptor.

Then, the pdptrace(2) was able to usefully control the target. A new ptrace call to retrieve the list of the attached processes PT_GET_CHILDREN allowed pdptrace(2) to get hold of forks.

With all the features implemented, it was possible to convert truss(1) to use only process descriptors to control the traced processes. The existing mode of using pids was preserved, and can be selected with the '-y' option as an emergency switch and to easy comparison and debugging of the new mode.

Changes affecting the base system and programs in it.

Contact: Olivier Certner Contact: Minsoo Choo

This quarter, a number of fixes and cleanups were merged to ULE and 4BSD:

Fix priority conflation of differently-niced CPU-bound threads (4BSD).

Fix priority diminishing too slowly when consuming CPU, because of some obsolete SMP scaling (4BSD).

Fix selecting lowest priority thread early in some corner cases (ULE).

Only allocate local runqueues (used for pinning/bound threads) for CPUs that are actually present (4BSD).

Removal of unused hlt_cpus_mask and sched_do_timer_acccounting().

Removal of unused kern.sched.4bsd.followon (4BSD).

When setting kern.sched.{4bsd,ule}.slice, check the value makes sense and make sure to update dependent internal constants such as hogticks and sched_slice_min.

Ensure sched_slice_min and the quantum computation stay sane for small quantum values (ULE).

Work is on-going and nearing completion on cleaning up the machinery allowing multiple scheduler implementations (a.k.a., "instances") to co-exist in the same kernel. From a single list of function descriptors, it now automatically produces the declaration of functions in the scheduler interface and in scheduler instances, the fields of the scheduler instance descriptor structure and the dispatching functions. A second round of changes is in preparation, with the aim to potentially remove implementation functions' namespacing (e.g., having ule or 4bsd in their names) in the source code, in effect renaming them back to their old names, which are those of the interface functions, while keeping the namespacing for C symbols which is required for debugging and in general manipulation by various ELF tools.

Work continues in the background on solutions to long-standing shortcomings in the ULE scheduler such as unfairness for non-interactive threads in certain particular circumstances and the very weak effect of nice values. For more information, please consult the previous report, and the slides of the latest presentation at EuroBSDCon2026âs DevSummit.

Links: D59275 URL: https://reviews.freebsd.org/D59275 rGaf25f2476230 URL: https://cgit.freebsd.org/src/commit/?id=af25f24762307bf606690c0aca6a3205a0515914

Contact: Devin Teske

truss(1) traces the system calls a process makes. Until this quarter it reported every call, which for anything larger than a toy program buries the calls of interest.

HEAD now accepts -t with a comma-separated expression naming the system calls to report. The option letter is the one System V Release 4 and SunOS truss use for this. A term may be a system call name, an fnmatch(3) glob (readlink*), a system call number in the traced processâs ABI, or @group for a family of related calls. A leading ! excludes what that one term matches and applies to no other termâââunlike SVR4 truss and Linux strace, where ! is sticky for the rest of the list. Terms apply in order; the last match wins. truss -t with no expression lists the groups and exits.

Groups are themselves -t expressions, so they compose without a second language. @desc is built from @read and @write rather than repeating their members. Member lists are patterns (extattr_*file, sctp*) rather than frozen name lists, so a later system call that follows the same naming convention joins the right group without a source change here.

Thirteen groups ship to start: @all, @creds, @desc, @file, @ipc, @memory, @net, @none, @proc, @read, @signal, @time, and @write. They are not a clone of Linux straceâs `% classes: @read and @write split descriptor data-in from data-out, and @time covers clocks, timers, and sleeping rather than clocks alone.

Show only the file and network activity of a command:

Show everything a command does except its memory management:

Show the descriptor activity of a running process apart from the data transfers themselves:

Count the readlink(2) and readlinkat(2) calls made while starting a program:

A system call excluded by -t is not decoded, so the filter also skips the cost of formatting arguments that would never be printed, and it is left out of the -c summary. Without -t, behaviour is unchanged.

The work is in HEAD as of af25f2476230, with an MFC planned after two weeks. Thanks to Robert Clausecker for review, and to Alexander Ziaee for the man page pass.

If a call you care about is in the wrong group, or a group you would use is missing, please write.

Links: D58066 URL: https://reviews.freebsd.org/D58066 rG3fe5961a0b70 URL: https://cgit.freebsd.org/src/commit/?id=3fe5961a0b708da599d42cbb6b5e4f030c28ea45

Contact: Devin Teske Contact: Faraz Vahedi

sysctl(8) speaks to the running kernel. sysrc(8) speaks to rc.conf(5). This quarter the set became three, and the new tool is a pleasure to use. sysconf(8) reads and writes the rest of the base configuration: loader.conf(5), sysctl.conf(5), and the make.conf(5) family (make.conf, src.conf, and src-env.conf). The syntax is the one your fingers already know. Given simply a name, reads back the value of the given name. name=value writes, and the reply comes back in the familiar line: name: old â new.

rc.conf(5) keeps the tool that already does it best. sysconf rc sshd_enable=YES hands every argument after rc straight to sysrc(8). One front door, and the right specialist behind it.

Under the utility is bsdconf(3), the figpar engine brought forward as one reader and one writer, co-authored with Faraz Vahedi. Each file family is a small descriptor: the keyword, the files, and the quoting rules of the program that will actually read them. Loader values are written quoted, because that is what the boot loader accepts. Sysctl values are quoted only when the round trip needs it. The make family keeps its real operators (+=, ?=, :=, !=) and the empty WITH_ / WITHOUT_ assignment, because for those knobs presence is the setting. You name the format with the target. -f names the path, so a loader-formatted file staged anywhere is still a loader file, and a generic target covers a file that matches no built-in.

Where the boot reads several files, sysconf reads those same files, in that same order. The loader target starts where the loader starts, at /boot/defaults/loader.conf, and follows loader_conf_files, loader_conf_dirs, and local_loader_conf_files, including a layout that points those lists somewhere else. The value you read is the value that takes effect. The value you write is stored where it will still take effect on the next boot. A removal clears every file that lists the directive, so that an earlier setting does not simply get unmasked. The same command lists the files and dumps the effective set:

-d reports the descriptions carried in the defaults file. -A widens a dump so directives still at their default are part of the picture.

A write replaces the file whole. The new text goes to a temporary in the same directory, is fsynced, and is renamed over the original, with mode and ownership preserved. If the machine stops halfway, the previous file is the one still on disk. Read-only use, a -c check included, runs inside a capsicum(4) sandbox: the files are opened, every other capability is dropped, and only then is a line parsed.

The sysctl target asks the running kernel before it stores anything. An unknown OID, a read-only OID, a loader-only tunable, or a value outside the typeâs range is reported and skipped, and a loader-only tunable is pointed at the loader target, where a boot setting belongs. Every other assignment in the same command still applies. On make and src, WITH_foo=no is written and you are told at once to use WITHOUT_foo=1 instead. That is the advice in share/mk/bsd.mkopt.mk, delivered at the keyboard, and repeated on a later read with the file and line so an old WITH_*=no stays in view.

-j and -R aim the same sentences at a jail or another root.

The introduction is in HEAD as of 3fe5961a0b70 (D58066), and sysconf(8) makes its first release in FreeBSD 16.0. It has already grown since that commit. A unique prefix of a target is enough (lo is loader, sy is sysctl, sr is src), and a poudriere target carries the same verbs to poudriere.conf and the make overlays under poudriere.d.

Thanks to Robert Clausecker and Faraz Vahedi for review, and to Alexander Ziaee for the release notes.

Try it on HEAD against a file you usually open by hand. If a format you live in is missing, please write. The descriptor layer is how the next one joins, and it would be good to hear which file you want next.

Links: Boot loader test framework URL: https://reviews.freebsd.org/D58008 XZ decompression for EFI memory disks URL: https://reviews.freebsd.org/D58073 Dynamic loader memory disks URL: https://reviews.freebsd.org/D59418 Independent EFI HTTP devices URL: https://reviews.freebsd.org/D59423 DHCP initial memory-disk option URL: https://reviews.freebsd.org/D59428 EFI chain-boot partition fix URL: https://cgit.freebsd.org/src/commit/?id=9ecc2493ca5fbba852e175674b5cb8975b99af84

Work this quarter expanded the boot loaderâs support for compressed images, memory disks, and HTTP network booting, with an eye to both iPXE integration, and loader.efi(8) completeness. It also introduced a QEMU-based test framework covering many of FreeBSDâs boot combinations.

The loader can now read files compressed with XZ or Zstandard in the same way that it already handled gzip and bzip2 files. XZ support is enabled by default in the BIOS and EFI loaders, including support for compressed memory-disk images such as FreeBSD installation images. Zstandard support is available as a build option.

Memory-disk handling was generalized so that the loader can create an md device dynamically. This provides a fallback on systems whose UEFI firmware does not implement the RamDisk protocol, a situation found on some smaller and embedded systems. The resulting memory disk is exported to the kernel and can contain both the kernel and the root filesystem. Downloaded memory-disk images now use the correct UEFI memory type, and downloads can be interrupted with Escape. This replaces the need to use the memdisk_uefi.efi third-party add-in that people needed previously for iPXE integration. Now loader.efi can also download images via iPXEâs download services, requiring only basic networking DXE modules in the UEFI firmware image.

EFI HTTP support previously depended on the firmware having loaded loader.efi through UEFI HTTP Boot and was restricted to the server selected by the firmware. The loader now accepts arbitrary http[N]://host[:port]/path device specifications. These can be used as rootdev, in loader.conf, or interactively, regardless of how the loader itself was started. The implementation can either reuse an existing loader network configuration or ask the firmware network stack to perform DHCP.

The DHCP client now requests a FreeBSD vendor option containing the URL of an initial memory-disk image. With this option, a machine can start loader.efi directly over the network, discover a detached root image through DHCP, retrieve that image over HTTP, and boot from it. Care was taken to transfer ownership of the network interface between the loaderâs native network stack and the UEFI HTTP stack. This is necessary because each stack needs different access to the firmwareâs network protocols.

A new tools/boot/boot-test.sh framework uses QEMU to test booting across aarch64, amd64, armv7, powerpc64, powerpc64le, and riscv64. It exercises the applicable BIOS, UEFI, OpenFirmware, and PReP environments with CD, MBR, GPT, network, and memory-disk configurations, as well as the Lua, Forth, and simple loaders. HTTP network-boot and gptboot.efi chain-boot tests were added later in the quarter. The framework is not yet an installed test because it builds and tests several target architectures from one host.

The chain-boot tests accompanied a fix for systems that use gptboot.efi to select between A/B system partitions. After being chain-loaded, loader.efi could skip the selected partition and boot the other system partition instead. The selected partition is now tried first, while the normal search of sibling partitions remains as a fallback. A separate loader change that interfered with some ZFS chain-boot configurations was reverted.

Other work added a loader.kboot(8) manual page, build knobs for omitting the x86 BIOS and userboot loaders from UEFI-only systems, and defensive checks for firmware that advertises unusable graphics output protocols.

Contact: Aymeric Wibo Contact: Olivier Certner

Suspend-to-idle and support for S0ix sleep is in the process of being added to FreeBSD.

This will allow modern Intel and AMD laptops, some of which do not support ACPI S3 sleep, to enter low power states to increase battery life.

amdsmu(4) now proactively diagnoses S0i3 entry after resuming from suspend-to-idle with a new eventhandler. If S0i3 was not entered, it will print the IP blocks that were blocking entry to dmesg, along with hints on how to resolve them.

The acpi_spmc(4) driver now checks Intel and AMD constraint packages. Malformed constraints are skipped instead of crashing.

Various improvements were made to the thunderbolt(4) driver: support for writing to router config space, controller resets, and a CRC accounting fix for config write messages. Thunderbolt controllers can now be resumed (in review), which allows multiple suspend-resume cycles without needing to reload the kernel module.

At this point modern standby works reliably on target laptops and most panics have been ironed out. The primary issue being worked on is GPE events generated while the machine is suspendedâââsuch as plugging or unplugging AC powerâââcausing panics.

Contact: Abhijeet Sharma

Clangâs -fbounds-safety lets C code state a bufferâs length, as in __counted_by(len). The compiler then checks accesses through that pointer. An out-of-bounds access traps instead of corrupting memory. The TCP/IP stack parses untrusted network input, so it is a good place to start. This project adds the macros and build support, then converts TCP files one at a time. Without the flag the annotations expand to nothing. The tree still builds with the base system compiler and with GCC.

External toolchain builds GENERIC on amd64, recipe on the wiki.

Macros, build knob and soft traps posted, four reviews accepted.

tcp_ecn.c runs checked, kernel boots and passes netinet tests.

mbuf accessor RFC on arch@ and net@, discussion ongoing.

Contact: Ishan Agrawal

PF uses Netlink to communicate between userland tools and the kernel, but before this work, truss(1) could not meaningfully decode the payloads of PF Netlink messages and would instead display much of the message as raw data.

This project adds a reusable Netlink payload decoding infrastructure to libsysdecode and integrates it with truss(1), allowing structured decoding of Netlink messages rather than exposing only their raw contents.

The core of the infrastructure is a generic attribute decoder based on decoder tables. The infrastructure supports decoding different attribute types, including integer values, strings, booleans, and nested attributes. Netlink commands can then provide their own decoder tables describing the attributes they contain, without requiring a separate decoding mechanism for each command.

The infrastructure has been used to add decoding for several PF Netlink commands, including PFNL_CMD_KILLSTATES, PFNL_CMD_GETRULES, and PFNL_CMD_GET_LIMIT.

For example, a PF Netlink message that previously appeared largely as an opaque buffer:

With the new decoding infrastructure, truss(1) can decode the Netlink message and PF payload into meaningful fields, for example:

truss(1) was also extended to track the protocol associated with AF_NETLINK sockets so that messages can be passed to the appropriate decoder. Netlink message flags are decoded as combinations of NLM_F_* flags, while unknown bits are preserved.

The work in this quarter established the infrastructure needed to continue adding PF Netlink payload decoders without duplicating parsing logic for each command.

This report focuses on the efforts using permissively licensed Linux wireless drivers, mostly unmodified, on FreeBSD, as well as preparing the native net80211 stack for support of newer standards.

A call for testing was put out for mt7921 based PCIe chipsets (MT7920E; MT7921E, also known as AMD RZ608; MT7922E ,also known as AMD RZ616). This is based on ongoing reviews, mostly to replace an old shortcut in LinuxKPI for struct page. Despite great interest in the driver the previous years we have not had a lot of feedback.

Work to support further mt76 chipsets will continue.

Thanks to the debugging of users the situation has slightly improved. It is expected that Linux v7.3 has a lot of bug fixes in the drivers but due to the timeline of Linux and FreeBSD release schedules may only hit main once again. Further issues have to worked on and fixed still.

In previous reports we have reported that this was blocked on a compiler option. During Q3 we found a way which can limit the scope to just LinuxKPI USB drivers. There is ongoing work to simplify the build framework for this. While there are rough edges still, especially around teardown and unplug we hope to put out a stack of changes for review or a tree for testing during October.

Initial work to remove workarounds from LinuxKPI and fix net80211 are ongoing.

The current upstream driver from Espressif Systems on Github v0.6 has been ported to FreeBSD. Initial changes to fix compiler warnings were submitted back as pull requests. The driver is currently awaiting a vendor import and to be followed by an unifdef within the FreeBSD tree as upstream supports a wide range of Linux versions. Special thanks go to Espressif Systems for providing me with two E22 sample cards in order to test the port.

During Q3 2026, a review of the bpf_movein() path in sys/net/bpf.c was conducted following an observed failure when writing to a BPF descriptor on lo0 (FreeBSD 14.4-RELEASE-p8).

The initial observation was a write(2) returning EAFNOSUPPORT when sending a packet through a BPF descriptor bound to lo0 (DLT_NULL). The original attribution â missing sa_len initialization in if_output drivers â was not sustained after independent review by Gleb Smirnoff.

Review established that the reproducer violated the DLT_NULL contract: a write(2) on a BPF descriptor must prepend a 32-bit word in host byte order containing the address family. The sa_len check proposed in the individual drivers (if_disc.c, if_gif.c, if_loop.c, if_me.c, if_tuntap.c) is not required because the existing BPF/ifnet interface contract is already defined at the BPF boundary in bpf_movein().

Following that review, D59140 was updated to add a defensive assertion in bpf_movein() per Glebâs suggestion:

This makes the existing BPF/ifnet contract explicit through a defensive assertion at the point where the contract is consumed. The assertion protects the sa_data bounds invariant at the point where the computed header length is consumed.

Identified and reproduced EAFNOSUPPORT on lo0 with BPF write(2) on FreeBSD 14.4-RELEASE-p8.

Submitted D59140 to Phabricator with initial fix targeting five if_output drivers.

Received review from Gleb Smirnoff identifying the reproducer defect: missing 32-bit DLT_NULL address-family header in the packet.

Corrected the reproducer and verified locally on FreeBSD 14.5-RELEASE.

Updated D59140 to replace the driver-level checks with a single MPASS assertion in bpf_movein() (Diff 186596).

Updated Summary and Test Plan in D59140 to document the complete investigation history: observed failure â initial attribution â independent falsification â corrected reproducer â local verification â upstream hardening proposal.

D59140 (Diff 186596) is under upstream review.

Await upstream review and disposition of Diff 186596.

Links: CAM lifecycle DTrace probes URL: https://reviews.freebsd.org/D58523 CAM peripheral invalidation events URL: https://reviews.freebsd.org/D58527 mpsutil discovery information URL: https://reviews.freebsd.org/D58528

Several changes this quarter made storage-device discovery easier to observe and diagnose, particularly during boot.

The CAM DTrace provider gained probes for peripheral I/O errors, error recovery, and peripheral invalidation. Additional probes report when CAM holds or releases the boot process and when a new bus is registered. Together these probes cover much more of the path from initial bus discovery through the creation of disk peripherals. They can also be used with DTrace anonymous tracing to investigate problems that happen before the system reaches multi-user operation. The new probes are documented in dtrace_cam(4).

CAM now sends a devctl(4) notification when a peripheral is invalidated. The notification includes the device serial number when available, or its CAM path otherwise, so system-management software can identify the device that disappeared. The common code used to construct CAM notifications was factored out to support this and future event types.

Two fixes improved the handling of disks that fail during probing. CAM now stops probing after a peripheral has been invalidated instead of sending more commands to an abandoned device, where they could cause long timeouts and confusing errors. A related condition for deciding when to invalidate a disk was corrected. Errors reported for NVMe disks through the CAM nda peripheral now identify the command set, making command opcodes easier to interpret.

mpsutil(8) gained a show discovery command that prints the controllerâs discovery tables. This exposes the controllerâs view of attached SAS devices and expanders and is useful when diagnosing devices that are missing or attached through an unexpected path.

Finally, nvmecontrol(8) received correctness fixes for Autonomous Power State Transition data. Transition values are now encoded without intermediate integer overflow, and identify data reporting an excessive number of power states is handled with a bounds check rather than an assertion.

Contact: Konstantin Belousov

Most non-x86 platforms are relatively strict with regard to the proper alignment of the data types. On the other hand, x86 ISA allows any alignment for the operands of integer scalar operations.

Still, there is an AC control bit in the processor flags register which causes alignment exception (fault) on unaligned operations. Practically the bit is not too useful because most of the compilers generate code that relies on the freedom of the working unaligned access on x86.

Particularly interesting case of the unaligned access is when the disposition of the operand causes it to span two cache lines (which is impossible for naturally aligned data). Normal (unlocked) operations cause so called torn reads and writes. This effect become observable starting with Core2 Intel microarchitecture.

Even more interesting case is provided by the locked operations using the LOCK prefix on read-modify-write instruction with the mis-aligned data. To satisfy ISA guarantees in this case, the CPU has to either take more than one cache line for exclusive ownership in MESI-like cache coherence protocol, or exercise so called bus lock ensuring global cache ownership. Either option has very high cost and causes observable detrimental effects on other processes and virtual machines executing on the same physical host.

Since some time Intel provides a control for the lock operations that need to span more than one cache line (split locks). Turning the control on causes split locks to generate the same #AC exception as done by the AC flag, but only for the split locks, instead of all unaligned accesses.

The feature is controlled by the platform MSR and is per-CPU global, which precludes making the MSR directly available to userspace. The new sysarch(2) operation I386_SET_SPLITLOCK was developed that enables the control for the calling thread. The control is part of the machine state maintained on the context switch.

The intent is mainly to assist in catching bugs where improperly alignment locking structures are created, unlike Linux, which uses the feature to artificially penalize such processes by slowing them down. If the program code modifications are not possible, users and administrators can LD_PRELOAD a trivial shared object that turns the control on.

Aquantia (now Marvell) AQtion devices are multi-gigabit PCIe Ethernet controllers supporting speeds up to 10 Gb/s. They are found on workstation and desktop motherboards, and add-in NICs.

Aquantia published a FreeBSD driver for its first-generation "Atlantic" controllers, but it was unmaintained for some time. FreeBSD developers contributed some fixes to the vendorâs repository, but several pull requests were never addressed. The driver was available in the ports collection as net/aquantia-atlantic-kmod, with some additional patches, but it was not part of the base system and lacked support for newer devices.

Ed Maste imported a snapshot of the vendor driver, applied patches from unmerged pull requests and the port, wrote an aq(4) man page, and connected it to the build.

Since then, Nick Price added support for the second-generation Atlantic 2 (AQC113) controllers, and has made extensive fixes and improvements throughout the driver. These include enabling jumbo frames, software LRO, and suspend/resume; correcting RSS queue distribution and honouring the kernel RSS policy; expanding and fixing checksum and VLAN offloads and VLAN/multicast filtering, hardening the attach, detach, reset, interrupt and RX/TX paths; handling PHY thermal shutdown; and improving diagnostics and link-state reporting.

The driver is available in -CURRENT snapshot images, and has been MFCâd to stable/15 to be included in FreeBSD 15.2.

Sponsor: The FreeBSD Foundation (Edâs work)

Updating platform-specific features and bringing in support for new hardware platforms.

This project adds FreeBSD support for three Banana Pi router boards: the BPI-R2 (MediaTek MT7623, armv7), the BPI-R64 (MediaTek MT7622, arm64) and the BPI-R2 Pro (Rockchip RK3568, arm64).

The Banana Pi BPI-R2 is a MediaTek MT7623N-based router board (quad-core ARM Cortex-A7, up to 1.3 GHz) with 2 GB DDR3, 8 GB eMMC, 4x Gigabit LAN and 1x Gigabit WAN driven by the built-in MT7530 switch, two SATA ports, two USB 3.0 ports, a mini PCIe slot, HDMI output, MIPI DSI/CSI connectors and the usual UART, I2C, SPI, PWM and GPIO headers. Because the MT7623 is an armv7 part, it is the only board of the three that is built from the 32-bit GENERIC kernel configuration.

Platform / machdep supportâââdevice map, early console, late init and SoC reset, plus the SOC_MEDIATEK kernel option and a DTB build for mt7623n-bananapi-bpi-r2.dts

Clock managementâââshared MediaTek clock infrastructure (gates, muxes, fixed factors) used by the topckgen, infracfg, pericfg, hifsys, bdpsys, imgsys, vdecsys and audsys clock controllers

System configuration registers (syscfg/syscon)

The Banana Pi BPI-R64 is a MediaTek MT7622-based development board (dual-core ARM Cortex-A53, ~1.35 GHz) featuring 4x Gigabit LAN, 1x Gigabit WAN, 802.11n 4x4 Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.0 and a range of peripheral interfaces (UART, SPI, I2C, GPIO, SATA, mini PCIe, eMMC and others).

PCIe configuration space driver (pciecfg)

sysirqâââthe interrupt polarity controller

SATA / AHCI, including SATA mode for the T-PHY

The Banana Pi BPI-R2 Pro is the next generation smart router development board, powered by a Rockchip RK3568 processor.

It carries 2 GB LPDDR4 memory and 16 GB eMMC storage, and offers two USB 3.0 ports, five Gigabit Ethernet ports, an M.2 Key-E and a mini PCIe slot, two MIPI DSI interfaces (one of which can be switched to LVDS in software), one MIPI CSI camera interface and one HDMI output.

ROCm is AMDâs compute platform, which is the set of libraries, drivers, and tooling used to program their AI accelerators, and/or GPUs. On FreeBSD there are only a few ways to run compute workloads (AI/ML, graphics, and so on) on the GPU, and to my knowledge those are Vulkan and OpenGL. Both are fine for graphics, and sometimes machine learning too, but a lot of workloads are just not well suited to them, and end up being done in ROCm or CUDA instead, since those give the developer a lot more control over how the task is actually executed.

So I have been slowly porting the ROCm toolchain over to FreeBSD, which would let the AI accelerator ecosystem run natively here.

Most of my time recently has been spent getting rocr-runtime working from my rocm-systems fork, whilst upstreaming the changes needed in the FreeBSD kernel. Once the kernel side is done, I can merge the amdkfd code into drm-kmod (after a lot of cleaning up), and from there it is mostly a matter of time getting the remaining pieces of rocr-runtime running.

The amdkfd driver now compiles, links, and loads.

Ported the v11 platform files for certain AMDGPU generations.

/dev/kfd is now exposed, and interactable.

Cleaned up undefined symbols which are not used as of now.

Refactoring all changes before doing a large upstream push of code which can be upstreamed.

The linux/util_macros.h` (D57465) has been committed to the kernel.

Added jiffies64_to_msecs (D58075) has been committed to the kernel.

Added compat_ptr_ioctl (D58076) has been committed to the kernel.

Added tgid to task_struct under LinuxKPI (D58228) has been committed to the kernel.

Various other LinuxKPI-related changes are still under review (D58207, D58222, D58845, D60275).

There have been about two pull requests accepted to rocm-systems, otherwise I am still working on the large one which merges in FreeBSD support. That code has not been completed yet, so I have not opened it.

Fixing initialisation issues in rocr-runtime, and working through whatever else shows up once it runs further.

Getting the large rocm-systems pull request finished and opened upstream.

Fixing issues with Sysfs within amdkfd. Still diagnosing issues, and figuring out what exactly the issue is.

If you have the cards and the time to test them, please reach out and I can tell you exactly how to do it.

The goal of this project is to improve OpenJDK support for FreeBSD/amd64 and FreeBSD/arm64.

Java is an important runtime environment for many high performance, critical enterprise systems. Making sure Java based applications run correctly and efficiently on FreeBSD is important to ensure that FreeBSD will continue to be a viable and attractive platform for enterprises, as well as businesses and organizations of all sizes.

This quarter, a few rather big, invasive features have been merged upstream (JEP 401: Value Objects and JEP 539: Strict Field Initialization), meaning that it has been difficult to get reviews and acceptance for our changes in this period. We have spent the time on fixing issues with the BSD port, as well as keeping it up to date with the upstream changes as they have appeared.

The following fixes/improvements have been done in this quarter:

Bug 296945: The wxneeded ELF flag is now set on the JDK binaries, allowing java to run on systems with W^X protection enabled.

Bug 294358: really build headless without installing Xorg libs

Removed USE_LDCONFIG from OpenJDK 8 and 11 ports. Fixes Bug 297282: java/openjdk25 - libjava.so does not find libjvm.so

Only return symbols that match the requested address for dladdr(3) on BSD. This also reverts the default visibility of libjvm symbols back to hidden to avoid exposing internal symbols. This should also make the library faster to load, and less resource hungry.

Submitted draft JEP for BSD port upstreaming effort.

Contact: Generic Rikka

This report continues the FreeBSD HPC Ports Modernization initiative, which aims to make FreeBSD a practical and maintainable platform for modern high-performance computing (HPC) software stacks. Previous quarters focused on bringing the Slurm, PMIx, PRRTE and UCX stack up to date and filling gaps in the surrounding ecosystem. This quarterâs work centered on three things: keeping the scheduler and communication libraries current (including security fixes), deepening FreeBSD-specific runtime support in UCX and enabling the Open MPI/UCX combination, and taking the first FreeBSD-native Slurm features upstream to SchedMD.

Updated sysutils/slurm-wlm three times, from 26.05.1 to 26.05.2 and then to 26.05.4, tracking upstream releases. The 26.05.4 update also addresses seven CVEs. Thanks to the configure-time HDF5 probe merged upstream last quarter, the obsolete downstream HDF5 patches could be removed and the downstream patch-configure was substantially reduced. The remaining FreeBSD conmgr patch was rebased and a missing include was added so the test suite builds on FreeBSD.

Enabled slurmrestd in sysutils/slurm-wlm. It had been disabled because it was believed not to build on FreeBSD, but with current Slurm it builds without any additional portability patches. The port now ships slurmrestd together with the REST/OpenAPI plugins.

Updated net/ucx from 1.20.1 to 1.22.0. Earlier in the quarter the port gained a guard around the Linux-specific netlink implementation, and ucx_vfs support was improved for FreeBSD by replacing fusermount3 with mount_fusefs/umount, using FreeBSD-compatible FUSE capability detection and fixing UNIX socket ancillary data handling (SCM_RIGHTS and peer credentials). A follow-up fix for the VFS inotify watch was contributed by Laurent Chardon.

Introduced a UCX option in net/openmpi, allowing Open MPI to be built against net/ucx on FreeBSD (work by Laurent Chardon, based on testing and reports from this initiative). This also fixed an OMPIO sharedfp/sm crash.

Updated benchmarks/py-reframe-hpc twice, from 4.10.0 to 4.10.2 and then to 4.10.3.

Updated sysutils/py-clustershell from 1.9.3 to 1.10.1, including fixes for unportable tests.

Submitted proctrack/freebsd-reaper to SchedMD, a new Slurm process-tracking plugin built on FreeBSDâs procctl() process-reaper APIs. The step daemon acquires reaper status, tracks descendants across process-group changes and nested reapers, and signals the tracked process tree during cleanup. On a FreeBSD test node it cleaned up orphaned, SIGTERM-resistant and nested children like proctrack/pgid, and additionally handled setsid, setpgid, double-fork and nested-daemon escapes, which proctrack/pgid does not. A zombie regression was retested and the node returned to IDLE without timing out or draining.

Submitted %o support for Include filenames in Slurm configuration to SchedMD. Include slurm-%o.conf selects slurm-FreeBSD.conf on FreeBSD and slurm-Linux.conf on Linux, so a heterogeneous configless cluster can keep one authoritative configuration on slurmctld. This has been running on a mixed FreeBSD/Fedora cluster using the corresponding port patches.

Addressing review feedback on the open UCX (UCS/SYS portability for non-Linux platforms) and mpifileutils (Linux-only API guards) upstream pull requests, to shrink the local patchsets of the ports further.

Following up with SchedMD on the proctrack/freebsd-reaper and configless %o Include submissions.

Land the outstanding upstream pull requests and keep identifying FreeBSD portability issues to fix upstream rather than patch locally.

Carry the Slurm patches accepted by SchedMD into the port and drop the corresponding downstream changes.

Continue tracking upstream Slurm, UCX, Open MPI, PMIx and PRRTE releases closely.

Document a reference Slurm + Open MPI + PMIx + PRRTE + UCX deployment on FreeBSD, including a mixed FreeBSD/Linux configless setup, to lower the barrier for new sites.

#10076. C++26 stumbles at finish line over Contracts dispute

ISO working group faces a fight over runtime checks, complexity, and the language's release timetable

The next version of the C++ programming language may be delayed at the last minute due to a dispute over a security-enhancing Contracts feature.

Contracts have deeply split C++ technical maintainers. One group backs the C++ creator Bjarne Stroustrup, who is against the technology in its present form in grounds it was hastily implemented. But others are eager to see Contracts implemented, even arguing the tech's detractors are poisoning the C++ development process itself.

The disagreement boiled over just before a vote to ratify the new version of the language.

In October, the Draft International Standard (DIS) of C++26 failed its ISO ballot — the next-to-last stage in the International Organization for Standardization’s approval process during which a standard's technical details are formally ratified by a set of national standards bodies.

The ballot saw 13 votes cast in favor, 9 against, and 12 abstentions, failing to meet the ISO requirement of having no more than 25 percent negative votes. Contracts was the major sticking point for those voting nay.

Contracts allow developers to add preconditions and postconditions to code, as well as assertions that check whether specified conditions hold. Such checks can help catch programming errors that might otherwise lead to undefined behavior.

Design by Contract has long been a feature of languages like Ada and Eiffel.

Developers have proposed adding Contracts  to C++ for at least a decade, after when they were abruptly yanked from C++20 owing to concerns over dangerous defaults.

But Stroustrup roasted the revised proposal (P2900) that made it into C++26.

“The P2900 contracts and extensions aim to change the nature of C++ and are an existential threat to C++, adding complexity and bloat,” Stroustrup and his colleagues wrote in a paper last August. They noted that the implementation is messy, outdated, not sufficiently tested, and could be more effectively implemented as a library.

Not everyone agrees. Andreas Fertig, a member of the C++ standardization committee, feels that the criticisms have already been vetted and that vetoing the proposal this late in the C++ release process is damaging to C++ itself.

“The topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting ‘no,’ an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken,” Fertig wrote in a blog post.

The elephant in the room is, of course, the ongoing criticism of how easy it is for developers to accidentally create security holes in C++, leading more than a few projects to adopt Rust. Adding controls might, as Stroustrup notes, hamper C++’s chief attribute of being a blazing-fast language.

Fertig accused Stroustrup and Co. of being sore losers.

“Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes,” he wrote. But in this case, “the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust."

Unlike Fertig, Harry Bott, CEO of the C++ Alliance – which maintains the open source EDG C++ compiler front end – does not see the Contracts discussion as disruptive to C++ itself.

“The draft being sent back isn’t a failure of the process—it’s the process working as intended,” he wrote to The Register by email. “That doesn’t mean the process can’t improve. The goal should be to learn from this and strengthen the process so C++ can continue to evolve in a way developers can rely on.”

With the ballot failing at this late point of the standardization process – a rarity in C++ history  – the language risks missing its expected shipping date of this year. That outcome may force everyone to refer to the new version as “C++27” rather than C++26. (That’s only the informal name; the official name of this eighth version of the language, should it be released next year, would be “ISO/IEC 14882:2027.”)

ISO C++ working group WG21 is meeting next week in Búzios, Brazil, for the confronto final.

According to a blog post from Thibault Ricord-Marchal, a software engineering consultant at the Paris-based Margo consultancy, the group faces a number of choices.

They can carve Contracts out of the spec so the rest of C++26 can ship. That will be messy work, though. The undo button has to be smashed on a lot of library hardening already done using Contracts.

Another option is moving Contracts into a separate technical specification, where work can continue to refine the technology.

Or they could do a minor revision, vote again and hope the balmy Brazilian weather chills everyone out.®

#10075. Same Cluster, 33 Points More Utilization: What Changed Was the Order

The previous post argued that utilization, not intelligence, is where the next real constraint in enterprise AI is forming, and it closed by noting that no playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. This is ours.

We built a constraint-aware GPU allocator and benchmarked it against a FIFO scheduler across seven benchmark scenarios. On identical hardware, running identical workloads, GPU utilization rose by as much as 33 percentage points, and priority-weighted output rose in every one of them, by as much as 105%. Nothing about the hardware changed. What changed was the order in which allocation decisions get made.

One note on measurement before the numbers start. Every gain below is expressed as improvement over the FIFO result on the same scenario. Utilization is reported in percentage points; value is reported as a percentage increase in priority-weighted output.

"Keep the GPUs busy" is not a decision a system can execute. The decision is narrower and much harder: which GPU runs which job, in which timestep, at what priority. Formally it is one binary choice per combination of GPU, job and timestep, and the output is a grid — every GPU, across the whole scheduling horizon, with a job name in each cell or nothing at all.

Four workload types compete for that grid: training, real-time inference, batch inference, and quantization. They split into two allocation shapes, and the split is where the difficulty lives. Training, batch inference and quantization are batch-like: once started, each needs a contiguous block of GPUs held without interruption until the job finishes. Real-time inference is the opposite: elastic, driven by a demand curve that changes every timestep, growing and shrinking as traffic does.

Two incompatible shapes competing for the same hardware in the same timestep is the core problem. A second heterogeneity sits inside a single type: for the same base model, training jobs range from a few hours to several days, and from one GPU to dozens.

The comparison point throughout is a FIFO-based scheduler: real-time inference served from a fixed reservation, and every other job placed in arrival order, without regard for priority.

Under the right conditions, that is a reasonable policy. When the cluster has slack, allocation order costs nothing in utilization, everything fits regardless of sequence, so FIFO and anything more sophisticated fill the same fraction of the pool. Contention is where that ordering cost stops being invisible and starts costing capacity too. It then becomes expensive in two separate ways, and they are worth taking one at a time.

The reservation. Real-time inference cannot wait for capacity; the GPUs have to be there the moment traffic needs them. A scheduler that places jobs in arrival order has no mechanism for releasing GPUs during a trough and reclaiming them before the next peak, so the only way to guarantee availability is to take each real-time application's maximum demand for the day and reserve that many GPUs for the whole day. The cost lands in every hour that is not the peak. An application needing six GPUs at midday and two at 4am holds all six for twenty-four hours, and the four idle GPUs are unavailable to any batch job for the entire day. They are not being used, and they are not free either. It is why the baseline sits near half the cluster in the two scenarios where reservation dominates: 51.6% in the mixed control and 53.6% in the training-heavy case. Roughly half a pool, with much of the idle half reserved rather than free. This cost is paid whether the cluster is contended or not — contention only makes it visible.

The ordering. Under real contention, which jobs fit at all depends on the order you place them, not just on how much capacity exists. Order is not a tiebreaker applied after the capacity question is settled. Order is a capacity decision. FIFO places each job as it arrives, without weighing what that job is worth and without checking what else still has to fit inside the horizon, so high-priority work waits behind whatever asked first and capacity gets committed in placements that later jobs cannot use.

The two compound. The block held for the day's maximum real-time demand is off the table for every batch job in the queue, in every hour, and whatever remains is handed out in the order the requests happened to arrive.

It is the GPU equivalent of an airline assigning aircraft to whichever charter called first, then finding nothing left to fly the route that actually pays. And GPUs reserved all day for a peak lasting a couple of hours are the grounded aircraft from the previous piece in the most literal sense: on standby, earning nothing, unavailable to anyone else.

[Figure: side-by-side allocation grids — allocator above, FIFO below, same scenario]

Across five benchmark scenarios built for genuine contention, the allocator improved both axes at once. Utilization moved from a 52–85% band to a 72–88% band. Priority-weighted value rose between 24.6% and 105.1%, averaging 52%. Every scenario, both metrics, no tradeoff to explain away.

The strongest single case was a training-heavy workload on 8 GPUs: utilization went from 53.6% to 87.0%, and value more than doubled, up 105%. Thirty-three points of a fixed, already-depreciating asset, recovered by reclaiming reserved standby capacity and placing the rest in priority order. (This figure reflect a single baseline ordering.)

The allocator removes both behaviors. Real-time demand is treated as a curve rather than a ceiling, allocated against demand at each timestep, with batch-like work occupying the troughs, bounded by the cap on how many GPUs a real-time job may swap between consecutive timesteps. And batch-like jobs are placed by priority across the whole horizon instead of in the order they arrived. The rest of this piece is how.

Utilization measures occupancy: what fraction of available GPU-time is allocated to something. It carries no information about what that something is worth. One scenario pulls the two apart completely, and the gap runs in a direction that is easy to miss.

In the scale test, 30 jobs across 64 GPUs, FIFO and the allocator produced identical utilization, 44.9% each, and identical throughput, 27 of 30 jobs completed. The allocator delivered 15.9% more priority-weighted value. Every dashboard reads the same. The cluster produced materially different output.

An objective that does not price priority can fill the cluster to exactly the same level, finish exactly as many jobs, and still deliver less. The previous piece argued that occupancy is a poor read on whether a cluster is earning; this is the measured version of that claim.

The alternative is not a longer list of heuristic rules. Some constraints only mean anything globally, and no local rule can express them: contiguous blocks, a budget for how much GPU churn is acceptable across the entire horizon, a guarantee that running work is never preempted. To honor those, the problem has to be written down as one thing.

Five constraints define a legal allocation:

The objective function has two terms. Allocating a GPU to a batch-like job earns a reward equal to its priority multiplied by a time-decay weight. Failing to meet real-time demand incurs a penalty proportional to the size of the shortfall.

The relative size of those weights is the entire service-level policy, expressed as one number. The real-time penalty weight is 5 to 10 times greater than the allocation weight. One unit of unmet real-time demand therefore costs what 5 to 10 GPU-timesteps of equal-priority batch work costs. The asymmetry is deliberate, and it means latency obligations are enforced inside the same optimization that places batch work, rather than by a separate autoscaler competing with the scheduler for the same GPUs.

It is also what makes the elastic treatment of real-time demand safe. The allocator can hand a GPU to batch work during a trough because underserving real-time demand later is priced so far above whatever that batch work earns — the penalty, not a static reservation, is what protects availability.

The time weight decays across the horizon for a reason that only makes sense in an online system: by the next scheduling run, new jobs will have arrived. Capacity used now is worth more than capacity promised later.

The formal model defines what a legal, well-scored allocation looks like. Answering an incoming request is a separate job, and it belongs to a separate component. This is NP-hard combinatorial allocation, and the scheduler is re-invoked every time a job arrives, so the decision has to come back in the gap between two API requests. That latency budget is the fixed constraint the architecture is designed around, which is why a heuristic sits on the hot path and the formal model sits behind it as the specification the heuristic is built to satisfy.

That heuristic is not a generic greedy allocator. Its rules are the formal model's structural constraints, which means every grid it produces is a legal allocation by construction. Not usually valid. Valid by design.

That design, applied across the whole horizon rather than one arrival at a time, is what produces the utilization gain. The allocator sees every queued job before it places any of them, it can hold the free pool in shapes the remaining work can actually occupy, a batch job needing a contiguous block of a given size still has room when its turn comes. Priority decides who gets first claim on that room. FIFO has neither view: it commits capacity to whichever job asked first, and a job that arrives later and needs a specific shape may find nothing left that fits, so it goes unscheduled and the GPU-hours it would have consumed go unclaimed.

It runs in 1 to 2 milliseconds on the five contended scenarios, and 15 milliseconds at 64 GPUs and 30 jobs — fast enough to run on every incoming request.

The system exposes two modes. Fast mode runs the allocator alone and returns its grid; this is the hot path. Full mode uses that grid as a starting point for the formal model, which attempts to improve on it — suited to periodic review rather than per-request decisions.

Utilization improved in every scenario but one, where it tied exactly. Value improved in all seven.

The scale test matters because it holds at size: 64 GPUs, 30 jobs, 15 milliseconds, 15.9% more value.

The uniform-priority test matters because it addresses the obvious skeptical reading. Override every job to identical priority, so that no priority signal distinguishes any of them, and the allocator still moves utilization from 76.8% to 87.5% and value up 23.1%. The gain is not purely an artifact of ordering by priority. Planning placements across the horizon contributes on its own.

Everything above assumes the scheduler knows how many GPU-hours each job needs and how much real-time traffic is coming. Both are predictions, not inputs, and a scheduler is only as good as they are.

A single generic estimator does not work, because the four workload types have qualitatively different cost drivers. This is where the specialization argument from the previous piece reconnects: the same logic that makes a task-specific model outperform a generalist applies to the estimators feeding the scheduler.

Training is not one workload. It varies along two independent, freely combinable axes. Strategy determines how much of the model is updated (full fine-tuning against parameter-efficient methods like LoRA). Technique determines the optimization objective and the training loop (SFT, DPO, RLHF, RLVR, CPT). The differences are not marginal: LoRA cuts trainable parameters by up to 10,000× and GPU memory roughly 3× against full fine-tuning, on the same base model. DPO removes both the reward model and the sampling loop of RLHF. Estimating from model size alone averages across runs that differ by orders of magnitude, in exactly the two quantities the scheduler decides on, duration and GPU count. Our training forecaster conditions on 22 features, including a categorical variable distinguishing 10 concrete training variants.

Quantization is a schedulable job, not a background chore. Quantizing a single large model can consume hours of GPU time on hardware that other work is waiting for. It gets its own forecast, built from calibration tiers by parameter count, with distinct handling per algorithm (bitsandbytes, AWQ, GPTQ) and a safety margin before rounding up to whole GPU-hours. Prior work in this area places quantization outside scheduling scope entirely.

Real-time inference is not estimated per job at all. It is forecast as a continuously recalibrated weekly demand profile, rebuilt from hourly traffic history and mapped to GPU counts under the same swap cost the formal model enforces. Forecast and optimizer therefore agree on what churn costs, rather than disagreeing and fighting each other. This forecast is what replaces peak reservation. A per-timestep demand curve is the only thing that lets the scheduler release GPUs during a trough with any confidence that they can be reclaimed before the next peak.

This closes back to the ordering argument. Better demand estimates are what make priority-aware placement possible in the first place, you cannot sequence jobs well without knowing what they will consume.

The obvious objection to all of this is that forecasts are wrong. What happens then?

The failure mode to avoid has a name worth borrowing: the end-of-world effect. An optimizer that cannot see past the end of its horizon makes present decisions that wreck the timesteps immediately outside it, because as far as the model is concerned, nothing exists after the horizon ends.

The architecture answers both problems at once. The scheduler optimizes a 24-hour horizon, but commits only the current timestep, and re-runs every 30 to 60 minutes. Run at 9am, and the 9am allocation is real; the plan for 10am through 5pm exists only so that the 9am decision is made by a model that knows a future exists. The real 10am allocation comes from the 10am run, against fresh data.

The consequence is that forecast error is absorbed by re-optimization instead of compounding. Each run inherits what is actually running and pins it in place, so successive plans update rather than thrash.

There is a secondary payoff. The horizon plan is itself a forecasting product: it surfaces real-time coverage risk and predictable idle windows before they arrive, which is useful whether or not those specific allocations are ever committed.

This is also why the time-decay weight exists. By the next run, the workload mix will have changed.

Airlines did not solve utilization by computing an optimal schedule. They solved it by encoding operational discipline into the order things happen (turnaround sequence, maintenance windows, crew rostering) and letting that discipline compound.

The same thing happened here. Thirty-three points of utilization in the hardest-packed scenario, and 52% more priority-weighted output on average, on the same hardware, with the same workloads, in a couple of milliseconds, came from encoding what the cluster physically permits into the order decisions get made. Structure beat sophistication.

The previous piece argued that specialization and orchestration are two halves of one problem: specialization shrinks what each workload needs, and orchestration decides where the difference goes. Neither lever pays off alone. This is what the second half looks like when it is built.

The GPUs were already installed, already committed, already depreciating. The gain was in how we chose to spend them.
