#10073. Palantir's NHS cancer app gets plenty of praise, precious few users

Official figures put uptake at just six trusts, while FoI responses raise questions about which are actually benefiting

Only a handful of NHS trusts are using the cancer app on the controversial £330 million Federated Data Platform (FDP) run by Palantir, while newly released figures raise questions about which trusts are benefiting.

Cancer 360 was designed to bring cancer patients' data from disparate spreadsheets and electronic health records into a central system, helping health professionals prioritize treatment.

Pilots began four years ago, and trusts are not charged directly for the FDP. Yet official figures put Cancer 360's uptake at just five or six trusts. Freedom of Information responses gathered by grassroots campaign group No Palantir in the NHS also reveal discrepancies between reported benefits and recorded use.

In June 2025, NHS England said that Cancer 360 "drastically cut down diagnosis times" and referred to a pilot at Chelsea and Westminster NHS Foundation Trust, which saw the proportion of patients diagnosed within 28 days climb from 72 percent to 85 percent.

The trust began trials in 2022, while working with Palantir under a £23 million contract awarded without competition, before the US firm was awarded the FDP contract in late 2023. Critics argued the FDP procurement was flawed as Palantir had developed use cases under £60 million in non-competitive contracts which were then carried over to the FDP.

Last year, NHS England said Cancer 360 served 46 registered teams and 239 active users, and processed 52,000 patients.

In June 2026, NHS England said there were five trusts using Cancer 360 as of March 2026. Of those, only two were listed as benefiting. In July, health minister Preet Kaur Gill repeated the five-trust usage figure in a Parliamentary answer.

Official data released in October said that as of June, six trusts were using Cancer 360 and five were benefiting, but did not identify the trusts or explain the increase. The stats have since been removed from the NHS England website but are archived here.

In June, NHS England responded to a Freedom of Information request. It said six trusts reported unique users logging into the Cancer 360 app over the last 12 months.

However, two trusts cited as having run successful pilots – Chelsea and Westminster Hospital and Royal United Hospitals Bath – were listed as having zero unique users logging into the system during that period, according to NHS England's reply.

Both trusts were said to have received benefits from the system, according to a FoI response sent to campaign group Foxglove in June this year.

The Register asked both trusts and NHS England to explain the discrepancy.

One of the six trusts said to be logging into the cancer app, East Lancashire Hospitals, reported just one unique user. It later confirmed in an FoI response in August that it was not live with the FDP. It had planned to adopt the platform, leading with Cancer 360, but did not have a date for going live with the app.

No Palantir in the NHS also identified trusts that considered Cancer 360 but decided against adopting it.

East Kent Hospitals University NHS Foundation Trust considered using the app but rejected it because there was "no immediate requirement for it," according to its FoI response.

In its FoI response, Bedfordshire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust said it did not adopt the app because of issues around the metadata requirements.

Meanwhile, official figures on cancer diagnosis waiting times show wider improvements across England. Given Cancer 360's limited uptake, those national gains cannot simply be credited to the app.

In July this year, the UK's statistical regulator told NHS England to ensure ministers are briefed accurately following a row over data used to promote the purported benefits of the Palantir-run FDP.

Campaign group Foxglove had found that nearly a third of NHS trusts using Palantir's health data platform were performing fewer patient procedures than before it went live and that Chelsea and Westminster Hospital accounted for 84 percent of the reported fall in outpatient waiting lists, while only 16 trusts were using the FDP tool. The Office for Statistics Regulation began assessing NHS England's claims about the FDP's performance and the quango included more caveats on its website.

Scrutiny of the FDP's reported benefits comes as the government decides whether to continue the Palantir-led contract beyond February 2027. The initial contract was provided for a term of up to seven years, with a maximum value of £330 million.

Reports this week suggest the government is set to renew the contract, but run a parallel procurement to find an alternative to Palantir as pressure mounts to reduce lock-in to a single vendor and boost sovereign technology.

Palantir was founded with startup money from a CIA-linked VC firm and has relied on close ties with the US intelligence, military, and immigration services since its inception, although its recent growth in the wider business market is notable. ®

#10072. How I accidentally became a millionaire

I am not a millionaire. I have never been one. And yet, if you were to ask Google about it, you might just walk away with the impression that I am.

Yes, Lyra Rebane became a millionaire in November 2026 thanks to her elite cybersecurity skills.

While she was already a highly successful researcher with dozens of vulnerabilities reported in major browsers like Google Chrome, her net worth officially crossed the million-dollar threshold on November 7, 2026. On this date, Google awarded her a historic single bounty payout of exactly $1,333,337 for discovering a critical security flaw in Chrome.

I am a hacker, though. I am a hacker with 14 Chrome CVEs. And I think I am a good hacker. But I don’t think I’m the bestest hacker. I don’t believe I’m capable of finding a vulnerability that’s worth over a million dollars. And even if I were, I don’t think Google would pay that much for a Chromium vulnerability.

Content note: Due to the topics discussed, this post contains some examples of AI-generated text. Those examples are clearly differentiated1. Everything else in this blog post is fully human-made - I do not use AI.

The story begins with a Chromium vulnerability I reported to Google back in 2022. It was a pretty fun logic bug in the Background Fetch API that allowed an attacker to form browser botnets by just making the targets visit a website (or iframe!).

Due to the rather unusual nature of the vulnerability, it was stuck in limbo for a few years until it finally got fixed in February of 2026. Google gave me a $1000 bounty, and a few months later the bug became public.

This bug has been closed for more than 14 weeks. Removing issue access restrictions.

Actually nevermind, turns out it was merely marked as fixed. And thus, yours truly appears in an article titled “Google publishes exploit code threatening millions of Chromium users”.

Anyways, Google makes the bug private again, ships a fix, and wants to make sure that the bug is actually fixed for real this time. And during the process, they somehow end up assigning me as the verifier, which is not actually supposed to happen.

So the way reporting security bugs in Chromium works is that your reports go to this platform called the Buganizer2. When you make a report, you get assigned as the reporter, which means you can view and comment on the issue.

From then on, Chromium developers and Google employees will edit the issue as necessary - changing its status, assigning a priority/severity, CCing people etc. One of the things they do is giving a bug bounty to the reporter, for which the VRP panel calculates a sum and then sets the vrp-reward field on the issue.

As an external reporter, you cannot edit any of those fields. But people set as the assignees, verifiers and collaborators can! And in this case, I was set as the verifier.

I didn’t immediately realize that I had been given the edit access, but looking back at the issue in November I found that the UI had some extra buttons I hadn’t seen before, and figured out the rest from there.

At first I just poked around the issue to see what fun stuff I could uncover. While doing that, I somehow managed to accidentally click on a sudden popup menu, which immediately assigned the issue to a bot account.

Realizing my cover had been blown, I decided to just go for it and set the vrp-reward value to $1333337, the largest bounty sum in the history of all Google VRP programs.

Having achieved my newfound wealth, I decided the next best step would be to announce it on the everything app3. I made my tweet in two parts - first, an announcement of achieving the record bounty, and then a video of me changing the vrp-reward value as the punchline.

We ❤️ 🐜🐞🦗🦟🦋. {echo,{{{Google,Chrome,Android,Abuse,Mobile,OSS,Cloud}Vulnerability,Patch}Reward,VulnerabilityResearchGrants}Program}

In just an hour, the joke tweet had already reached 600 likes. Since my intent was to just make a joke and not actually deceive anyone, and the tweet was clearly escaping containment, I followed it up with a clarification.

Now, Twitter does actually have a feature to combat disinformation - Birdwatch (aka Community Notes) is a system that lets people add context to misleading posts. And this feature was in fact used on my tweet - in just a couple hours, the likes stopped rolling in, and this funky box appeared underneath.

Proposed by an experimental AI contributor responding to requests for a note. Like all contributors, AIs can make mistakes — verify accuracy.

The $1,333,337 Chrome VRP bounty claim is false; the author edited the screenshot themselves as a joke after gaining mistaken edit access and Google awarded no such reward. https://x.com/rebane2001/status/2119193210513936644 https://piunikaweb.com/2026/10/15/google-250k-bounty-ai-chrome-exploit-xbow/ https://bughunters.google.com/blog/google-vrps-in-review-2025

And this would’ve been the end of it, if it wasn’t for the fact that Elon4 completely fucked up the Community Notes system! You see, this note here was generated by an “experimental AI contributor”, and thus, it claimed that I had “edited the screenshot [myself]”, which was simply not true!

This made me unhappy. And what do we do when we’re unhappy? We tweet about it5!

And thus, pretty soon, the community note disappeared.

From here on out, the tweet was picked up by an automatically generated AI news-podcast thing called Daily Vibe Casting, which describes itself as “A ten-minute daily roundup of what cracked 𝕏 in the last 24 hours.” Or in other words, it throws trending tweets into a chatbot.

@rebane2001 says a Chrome vulnerability they6 discovered earned $1,333,337, which they describe as the largest award in Google’s Vulnerability Rewards Programme. The post does not explain the flaw, so there is little basis here for judging its scope or technical impact.

The payout is striking on its own. Browser security depends partly on researchers finding problems and reporting them, and an award this size puts a substantial price on that work.

This text is AI-generated · Original article

I now had a viral tweet and an AI-generated “news” article - both of which claim I made a million dollars and show up in Google’s search results.

The largest recorded Chrome bug bounty is $1,333,337, awarded to security researcher Lyra Rebane in November 2026 [Post on X].

Would you like to know more about how Google's VRP reward tiers work or details on other recent high-payout security vulnerabilities?

Lyra Rebane does not offer reward tiers. However, if she hypothetically owned a hotel chain, the reward tiers would be as follows.

However, this is just a hypothetical scenario and Lyra Rebane does not operate a hotel chain. Would you like to instead learn about recent high-payout security vulnerabilities or the $1,333,337 chome bug bounty?

Sorry, I cannot assist you with this topic because you haven't passed our Hacker Reputation Test. To do the HRT, you must submit a list of CVEs you have been credited for.

Would you like me to tell you more about buying CVE accreditation, or do you want to learn about how Google's VRP reward tiers work?

my chrome vulnerability was just awarded the highest bounty in @GoogleVRP history - $1333337.Missing: largest | Show results with: largest

17 minutes ago — Researcher Rebane says the $1,333,337 payout is the largest in Google's Vulnerability Rewards Program. Daily Vibe Casting's Avatar.

And there it was! My little stunt turned into something that Google’s AI believes and makes into a story shown to every person searching for the highest Chrome bounty. And looking up my name now tells you about me being a millionaire!

There are a bunch of screenshots of this from other people under this thread. I’ve also seen cases of this affecting ChatGPT as well as Kagi Assistant.

So that is the end of my fun little story. I doubt it was particularly surprising to anyone, but I think it’s a good case study on how both social media platforms and people’s reliance on AI can be abused to distribute disinformation and cause harm.

This example here, of course, is mostly harmless and just something that happened on accident - I wasn’t attempting to mislead people, and it’s not really my fault that Google’s AI didn’t read my replies in the Twitter thread.

One could argue that I’m a reputable security researcher with a track record of posting truthful information, so this is all moot anyways because I am trustworthy.

But I think this here demonstrates just how fragile and easily abusable our information channels are. If I was a threat actor looking to spread disinformation, how difficult would it be to pull something like this off intentionally?

There are many ways to game Twitter. Its algorithm is publicly available, and people have figured out what kind of engagement results in what kind of algo boost. Bigger accounts can boost tweets and accounts significantly more7, so if you’ve got a few of those you can bootstrap new accounts way easier. But you can also just make bot accounts and slowly work your way up. And if you’ve got a bunch of accounts with reach you win.

And oh boy are there a lot of bot accounts! Look at, for example, the tweet this blogpost is about. There are a lot of obvious bot accounts in the replies. Maybe those very same accounts are also building reputation and voting on random community notes?

It’s kind of crazy to me that I could just post a tweet and have a community note removed. While the community note was actually wrong on a technicality, I’m sure there isn’t much preventing a bad actor from doing the same thing I did.

If I were a bad actor, I’d post disinformation that’s difficult to accurately disprove. If a community note doesn’t have a good source, or if it’s highly likely to get details wrong, it either won’t appear, or will have an easier time disappearing.

And all you really need to do is get a few tweets with specific keywords trending, and you’ve poisoned the search results, which then also poisons the AI.

And while you specifically might not take the AI Overview at face value, I’d guess that a lot of people do. It’s the first thing that shows up, it’s big and flashy, and it’s often unclear whether the only source of information is a tweet.

Tweets can mislead humans too, of course, but I feel like someone searching for something wouldn’t blindly trust a single tweet in the search results.

Note: While reading this post you may have tried to recreate the results I’ve shared, but without much success. The reason is that by now, my tweet has another community note on it, which Google picks up on and refers to the $1,333,337 bounty as a “prank”.

#10071. Multi-Vector (Late Interaction) Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v6.0 update, it gains a fourth model type: MultiVectorEncoder, for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval. Any PyLate checkpoint and any Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint loads straight into it, and colpali-engine models for visual document retrieval can be used too, through the same familiar API you already use for dense, sparse, and reranker models.

Where a regular embedding model compresses a whole text into one vector, a multi-vector model keeps one vector per token and scores query against document with the MaxSim operator. That preserves token-level matching information that a single vector has to average away, which usually means stronger retrieval at the cost of a bigger index. It's also the state of the art for visual document retrieval, where a text query is matched against page images directly, with no OCR step in between.

In this blogpost, we'll show you how to use these models: loading the various checkpoint formats, encoding and scoring, plugging them into a search stack, running them on page images, and keeping the index affordable. Everything below runs on a plain pip install -U sentence-transformers.

This blog is about using multi-vector models. If you want to learn how to train them, see the companion Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost.

A dense embedding model reads a text and returns a single fixed-size vector. Everything the model noticed has to fit in those 384, 768, or 1024 numbers, and similarity is one dot product between two such summaries. This works remarkably well, but the compression is lossy in a specific way: a rare entity, an exact identifier, or one crucial clause in a long passage all have to compete for room in the same vector. A query with several requirements at once runs into the same wall. For "green sofa with wooden legs and rounded cushions", a single vector has to blend all four into one point, so a green sofa with the wrong legs ends up sitting close to the one you actually asked for.

A multi-vector model (also called a late-interaction or ColBERT-style model, after the ColBERT paper) skips that compression. It runs the same transformer, but instead of pooling the token embeddings into one vector, it projects each token embedding down to a small dimension (classically 128) and keeps all of them. A 9-token document becomes a 9x128 matrix, not a 1x128 vector.

The interaction between query and document is then deferred until scoring time, which is where the name "late interaction" comes from. A cross-encoder interacts early, with both texts going through the model together, which is accurate but leaves nothing to precompute, since every document has to be re-encoded for each new query. A bi-encoder, which is what the dense embedding model above is, barely interacts at all (one dot product between two finished summaries), and that is exactly what lets you encode a collection once and query it fast. Late interaction sits in between. Documents are still encoded independently and can be indexed offline, but scoring compares every query token against every document token, which leaves far more room for the two to interact.

Scoring uses MaxSim: for each query token, take its highest similarity against any document token, then sum those maxima across the query.

MaxSim(Q,D)=∑Qi∈Qmax⁡Dj∈DQi⋅Dj\text{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{Q_i \in Q} \max_{D_j \in D} Q_i \cdot D_jMaxSim(Q,D)=Qi​∈Q∑​Dj​∈Dmax​Qi​⋅Dj​

Because the token embeddings are L2-normalized, each of those dot products is a cosine similarity in [-1, 1], so the whole sum lands within [-num_query_tokens, num_query_tokens].

You can read the operator as a soft alignment, where every query token points at the one document token that best explains it, and the score is how well the document supports the query overall.

The alignment doesn't have to be lexical, since the token embeddings are contextualized. Encode "Where do penguins live?" against "Penguins inhabit Antarctica." with lightonai/mLateOn and the query token live finds its best match on inhabit at 0.94, a word it shares no characters with! That is the thing lexical retrieval cannot do, BM25 and its relatives need the term itself, so synonyms and paraphrases slip past them. Dense embedding models bridge that gap as well, of course. What late interaction adds is that it does so without giving up the other direction. When an exact match is what matters (a product code, a surname, a function name), MaxSim still has that token sitting there on its own, where a single-vector model had to average it in with everything else. It isn't one-to-one either, since several query tokens routinely settle on the same document token.

You gain retrieval quality, particularly on queries where one specific piece of a document is what makes it relevant, on multi-requirement queries like the sofa above where each requirement gets to find its own evidence, and on out-of-domain data where a dense model's compression was tuned for a different distribution. That compression is learned from the training queries, so the model learns to keep what they needed and drop everything else, which may include exactly what your production queries ask about. The effect grows with document length, since more text has to fit in the same fixed vector.

The cost is index size. One vector per token instead of one vector per document is a lot more vectors, only partly offset by the smaller dimension. Encoding 4,874 Natural Questions passages with lightonai/LateOn produced 608,414 token vectors, an average of 124.8 per passage:

That's about 42x the storage of the MiniLM index, or 62 KiB per passage. However, indexes are often compressed, e.g. the same 608,414 vectors take 92 MB as a fast-plaid index, since PLAID stores a centroid id plus a quantized residual per vector rather than the vector itself. For scale, a 4096-dimensional dense model like Qwen3-Embedding-8B would need about 80 MB for these same 4,874 passages, so a compressed multi-vector index sits in the same territory as the dense indexes people already run. Token Pooling cuts the vector count before any of that, and Retrieve and Rerank avoids building an index at all.

PyLate comes up throughout this post, so here is the short version. Sentence Transformers handled dense and sparse models but not late interaction, so LightOn built PyLate on top of it to close that gap, adding the training, inference, and retrieval pieces these models need. Much of what you'll load below was trained with it, and LightOn built an ecosystem around it too, including fast-plaid, the late-interaction index that turns up in Indexing. With v6.0 those capabilities live in Sentence Transformers itself.

With the tradeoff in mind, let's get a model running.

Multi-vector models work with a plain install:

For ColPali-style visual document retrieval, you also need the image dependencies (see Installation for all extras, and Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models for multimodal support in general):

Sentence Transformers v6.0 requires transformers v5.x, torch 2.2+, and huggingface-hub v1.x. If you pin any of those lower, plan the upgrade first. See the Migration Guide for the full list of breaking changes.

Loading a multi-vector model looks exactly like loading any other Sentence Transformers model:

To find models that work, look for the multi-vector and sentence-transformers tags on the Hub. Any model with those tags loads with the line above, whether it started life as a PyLate checkpoint, a Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint, or a ColPali-family model for visual document retrieval. We're working through the ecosystem to get that tag onto every model that works, so the list keeps growing.

Underneath, MultiVectorEncoder reads each of the formats these checkpoints have been published in over the years, so PyLate and Stanford-NLP checkpoints load directly even where the tag hasn't been added yet:

Visual document retrieval models are the exception. ColPali-family checkpoints ship in colpali-engine's own format, which carries no information Sentence Transformers can use, so each one needs a small configuration added to its repository before it loads. Most of that work is done and waiting to be merged. See Supported Models for the current state and how to load them today.

Multi-vector models carry a handful of recipe knobs that differ per checkpoint: marker prefixes for queries and documents, length caps, whether queries are padded out with [MASK] tokens, and which tokens are skipped when scoring documents. All of them live in the module configs, so print(model) shows you exactly what you loaded. Here's the original ColBERTv2 checkpoint, which pads every query to exactly 32 tokens and truncates documents at 180:

That's the classic ColBERT pipeline: a Transformer producing contextualized token embeddings, a token-level Dense projecting each of them to 128 dimensions, a MultiVectorMask deciding which tokens count during scoring, and a token-level Normalize. Other checkpoints fill in different values. lightonai/GTE-ModernColBERT-v1 uses the same four modules with [Q] and [D] prompts, no query expansion, and caps of 48 and 300.

You rarely need to touch any of this, since every released checkpoint configures its own. It matters when you build a model from a bare backbone, which is covered in Creating Custom Models.

One value is worth checking against your own data, though. document_length truncates, so anything past it never reaches the index. For example, a 662-token passage through LateOn's cap of 300 comes back as 273 vectors, with the rest of the passage simply gone. Most of these checkpoints were trained on short passages, so if your chunks are longer than the cap, you can lift it for a single call with encode_document(..., processing_kwargs={"text": {"max_length": 512}}), keeping in mind that you would be running the model past the length it was trained on and that the index grows roughly in proportion. Multi-vector models tend to tolerate that well. On MLDR, a long-document retrieval benchmark, the multilingual siblings of the pair above show the gap clearly: mLateOn scores 77.92 against mDenseOn's 51.59.

Multi-vector models are asymmetric, so queries and documents go through different prefixes, different length caps, and different scoring masks. Unlike many dense models, where the two are interchangeable, encode_query() and encode_document() are required to get correct embeddings:

What you get back is a list of 2D tensors, one per input, each of shape (num_tokens, embedding_dim). Unlike dense embeddings, you can't stack these into one rectangular tensor, because every input has its own token count. The second document is longer than the first, so it comes back as a taller matrix.

Each call applies the model's own recipe for you. encode_query prepends the query marker, expands the query to a fixed length if the checkpoint asks for it, and caps it at the query length. encode_document prepends the document marker, caps at the document length, and drops any skiplisted tokens (punctuation, for most checkpoints) from the scoring mask.

The usual encode() arguments all still apply, so batch_size, show_progress_bar, convert_to_numpy, device, and multi-process pools work the way you'd expect:

model.similarity() computes the full all-pairs MaxSim matrix:

Mars wins, as it should, though the runners-up are close behind. Saturn also contains the literal phrase "the Red Planet", and Jupiter is a planet with a red spot, so a token-level operator has plenty to latch onto in all three. The ordering is what matters.

Scores often sit this close together, as GLInt shows by measuring the spread across a full candidate pool. MaxSim takes a maximum per query token, so a document will usually give every query token some decent best match, and scores start from a floor. Contextualized token embeddings are also anisotropic, clustering in a narrow cone rather than spreading out, so even arbitrary token pairs tend to score high.

There is also model.similarity_pairwise(), for when you already have matched pairs and just want the pair scores instead of the full similarity matrix:

MaxSim sums over query tokens, so its magnitude scales with how many query tokens there are, which means you can't compare scores across models with different query recipes. LateOn encodes the Red Planet query above as 12 tokens. Run that same query and those same documents through ColBERTv2, which pads and truncates every query to exactly 32 tokens, and the scores land in a completely different range:

Within one model the ordering is all you need, but if you want scores on a bounded scale, switch the model's similarity function to MeanMaxSim, which divides by the query token count. Back on LateOn:

Now every score is an average cosine similarity in [-1, 1], although you'll only see [0, 1] in practice.

If your corpus is small, exhaustive MaxSim over all of it is the simplest thing that works. Encode the corpus once, then score each query against everything:

Those 4,874 passages encoded in 20 seconds on an RTX 3090, and each search takes about 120ms end to end, most of that the MaxSim scoring against all 608,414 token vectors. This is exact, but it scales linearly in total corpus tokens and keeps every token vector in memory, so reach for it when you have a few thousand documents rather than a few million. The runnable version of this script is semantic_search.py.

Past that size you want a real late-interaction index, which Sentence Transformers doesn't ship. It doesn't need to, because these indexes store whatever encode_document produced, so you encode here and hand the token embeddings to something built for them. Indexing has working snippets for four of the options, and the section directly below covers how to skip the index entirely.

You can also get late-interaction quality without maintaining a late-interaction index, by using a multi-vector model as your reranker. A fast bi-encoder narrows a large corpus to a handful of candidates, then the multi-vector model rescores only those:

Only the 50 candidates are ever encoded as multi-vectors, so your index stays a normal dense index and the token vectors are transient. This is the same role a cross-encoder plays in a retrieve-and-rerank stack, but a multi-vector model is considerably cheaper per candidate. You encode the documents in one batch and score them with a matrix multiplication, instead of one forward pass per query-document pair. The runnable script is retrieve_rerank.py, which prints the timings of both stages.

Several vector databases index and score multi-vectors natively: Qdrant since v1.10, Weaviate since v1.29, Vespa for years now, LanceDB since v0.15.0, and VectorChord, which adds a MaxSim operator to Postgres that plain pgvector doesn't have. Milvus joined them in v2.6.4, under array-of-structs rather than the unrelated feature it calls multi-vector search. If you would rather not run a server at all, LightOn's fast-plaid is a pip install away and implements PLAID directly, and PyLate wraps it in a fuller retrieval stack.

A few others get you partway. OpenSearch and Elasticsearch can rescore candidates with MaxSim but not retrieve on it, and the Elasticsearch field is additionally in technical preview and Enterprise-tier. turbopuffer has late-interaction indexing in private beta.

The snippets below index text, but nothing in them is text-specific. encode_document hands back the same list of token-vector matrices whether the document was a passage, a page image, an audio clip, or a video, so the ColPali-style models from Visual Document Retrieval go into any of these unchanged. There are simply more vectors per document, which is what makes Token Pooling worth reaching for sooner there.

fast-plaid, Qdrant, Weaviate, and Vespa all take exactly what encode_document returns, so the code is the same up to the client library. Here's a working snippet for each, run against the 4,874 passages and 608,414 token vectors from the Semantic Search example. Each one carries the ingestion and query times it produced on one machine (RTX 3090, i7-13700K), with no tuning beyond what the code shows, to give a sense of the shape of the work. All four answer the query faster than the 98ms model.similarity took in that section, and three of them do it on the CPU, since fast-plaid is the only one here using the GPU.

All four returned the same three passages in the same order as the exhaustive PyTorch MaxSim earlier in this post, and the three databases reproduce its scores to four decimals! That is because their snippets score every document, which is affordable at this size and removes approximation as a variable. fast-plaid is approximate by design, so its scores differ slightly. The notes under each one say what changes when you switch to an approximate index, which is where rankings start to drift.

fast-plaid is LightOn's Rust implementation of PLAID, the index ColBERT was originally built around. There's no server to start, and it reads the tensors encode_document hands back without any conversion.

The index argument is a directory, not just a label, so the index is written to disk as it is built. Pointing a new FastPlaid at the same path reopens it for searching or for adding more documents, instead of rebuilding from the embeddings each time. On this corpus it occupies 92 MB, against 311.5 MB for the raw float32 vectors.

This is the only one of the four that is approximate, and it is the one place in this section where the scores do not match the exhaustive MaxSim. PLAID prunes with centroids and stores quantized residuals, so the three scores drift by a few hundredths in both directions against the 11.9192 / 11.7591 / 11.6710 computed earlier. The ranking is unaffected here, and that is the trade PLAID is making. It was designed for corpora far larger than this one, where scanning everything is not an option.

Qdrant needs a server: docker run -p 6333:6333 qdrant/qdrant. The client also has a local mode (QdrantClient(":memory:")) that needs no server, but it's a pure-Python reimplementation, so use it for trying things out rather than for timing them.

MAX_SIM is the only comparator Qdrant offers, and hnsw_config=HnswConfigDiff(m=0) is their recommendation for late-interaction fields, since the vectors are used for rescoring rather than graph traversal. Note that Qdrant themselves suggest reserving late interaction for reranking a few hundred candidates rather than scanning a whole collection, which is the Retrieve and Rerank pattern. At 4,874 documents the full scan costs 18ms and is exact, but that doesn't extrapolate.

Weaviate needs a server too: docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 50051:50051 cr.weaviate.io/semitechnologies/weaviate:1.34.0. Multi-vector support needs 1.29 or newer, and the embedded mode isn't available on Windows.

Defaults are enough here. Weaviate's dynamic ef resolves to 100 for a top-3 query, and this ranking is already exact from about 32 upward. That margin is a property of the embeddings rather than of Weaviate, so it's worth confirming on your own model instead of assuming the defaults hold.

Weaviate also supports MUVERA encoding, which made ingestion 3x faster and queries 1.8x faster in our test. It cost far more accuracy than that speed is worth at this size though, since the correct third passage didn't appear even in its top 50.

Vespa also runs in a container, but pyvespa starts it for you, so there's no separate docker run.

Vespa asks for the most upfront structure of the four, because you're declaring a ranking pipeline rather than just an index. In exchange you get to write MaxSim out as a tensor expression and see exactly what it computes. This version puts MaxSim in first-phase over where true, which scores all 4,874 documents and is why the output matches exhaustive MaxSim exactly. It's deliberately not what Vespa recommends at scale. Their ColBERT sample app stores int8-binarized vectors and moves MaxSim into second-phase to rerank a cheaper first stage.

Moving to that phased setup needs care, because second-phase rescores only the best 100 candidates by default, and here that window left two of the three correct passages unscored entirely. Raising rerank-count to cover your candidate set fixes that, though at this size the phased version still came out slower than simply scanning everything.

Late interaction is the state of the art for visual document retrieval, matching a text query against page images, with charts, tables, and layout intact, and no OCR step. This is what the ColPali family of models does, and those checkpoints load and run through the same API, with the revision pinning the open pull request that adds this one's Sentence Transformers configuration (Supported Models has the full list). Image documents are passed as URLs, local paths, or PIL images:

Each query retrieves its own page (the diagonal), and the second query separates much more cleanly than the first, since only one of the four pages is about outlay over time.

The code is unchanged. Underneath, the processor handles the visual prompt and the image patches, and MaxSim scores query text tokens against document image patches. A page holds many separate regions, which is exactly what makes late interaction a natural fit here, since a single vector would have to average a chart, a table, and three paragraphs into one summary. That fidelity costs index space, though. The shapes above are 755 token vectors for one page against 25 for the query, where a Natural Questions passage from earlier averaged about 125, so token pooling is worth reaching for earlier here than it is for text.

These are VLMs, so plan for the memory they need. The table in Supported Models runs from 252M to 8.8B parameters, and the small end of it stays practical on CPU where the multi-billion ones don't.

Page images are the common case, but they're not the only non-text modality. Sentence Transformers accepts text, images, audio, and video, and a checkpoint supports whichever of those its processor does, which model.modalities reports. A single document can combine modalities too, by passing a dict like {"text": ..., "image": ...} in place of a bare value. Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models covers multimodal models in Sentence Transformers more broadly, and the Usage documentation lists exactly which input formats each modality accepts.

vidore/colqwen-omni-v0.1 is built on Qwen2.5-Omni and takes all four modalities. Retrieving a recorded conversation with it is the same two calls as retrieving a page:

ColQwen-Omni was trained purely on image-text pairs, so its audio retrieval is zero-shot. It never heard a training example, and there is no transcription step anywhere in the pipeline. The query says nausea where the recording says carsickness, and it still picks the pharmacy conversation out of twenty by a wide margin.

Video works the same way, but sample the frames or it will eat your VRAM. Its release blogpost is blunt about this, that video "is very memory-intensive, so it's best suited for short clips":

At 1 fps and full resolution the same pair of videos produces 8,426 and 5,137 token vectors and peaks at 20.8 GB of VRAM, against 4,240 and 2,446 vectors and 12.5 GB here, for a model that occupies 9.0 GB on its own. The ranking is identical either way. Long audio wants the same treatment, and the release blogpost recommends 30-second chunks, which come to roughly 800 tokens each.

Because MaxSim is a sum of per-query-token maxima, a ranking decomposes exactly, so every point of a document's score belongs to one query token and one document token. That lets you answer "why did this rank here?" precisely, rather than by eye.

For image documents, sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.interpretability overlays that decomposition onto the page as the standard ColPali heatmap, either aggregated over the query or one map per query token. Asking "How much was spent on water resources and power?" against the outlays page from above, this is where the water token went:

heatmap.py is the runnable version, including the masking step that lines the document embedding up with the patch grid.

Text documents have no patch grid to overlay, but the same decomposition applies. text_similarity_map.py ranks a corpus and then attributes the top hit's score token by token, here on the Natural Questions corpus from earlier with the 32M-parameter mxbai-edge-colbert-v0-32m:

rich, mond, preliminary, and final matched themselves, while when settled on since and play on game. Three special tokens contribute 22.7% of the score while carrying none of the query's content. Below this table the script prints the passage itself, with the winning tokens highlighted in place.

If the index footprint worries you, the most effective knob is to store fewer token vectors. HierarchicalTokenPooling implements the token pooling technique from Clavié, Chaffin, and Adams by clustering each document's token vectors with Ward linkage on cosine distance and replacing each cluster with its mean, keeping roughly 1 / pool_factor of the tokens. Within one document a lot of token vectors end up close to each other, so much of what you drop is redundancy rather than signal:

There are three places to apply it, depending on when you want to pay for it:

By default, pooling applies to documents only, since queries are short and are the side you can't afford to distort. On the Natural Questions corpus from earlier, the reduction tracks pool_factor closely, and pooling all 608k token vectors took about 6 seconds:

A cluster mean is a worse match for a query token than the best of its members was, and the coarser the clusters, the more that shows. The original experiments measured that cost on BEIR and found very little of it, at 100.6% of the unpooled retrieval performance on average at pool_factor=2, and 99.0% at pool_factor=3. Halving your index for free is a good deal, so 2 is a reasonable place to start. How much it costs on your data is corpus-specific though, so measure it with an evaluator before you settle on a factor. The runnable comparison is token_pooling.py.

How far you can push pool_factor is also partly a property of the model. LightOn's hierarchical pooling regularization trains for exactly that, shaping the embedding space so pooling costs less and reporting 99.4% retention at 5x compression. Training with that regularizer isn't in Sentence Transformers yet, but the resulting checkpoints are ordinary PyLate models, so lightonai/LateOn-hpool-regularized loads and pools like any other.

Multi-vector models run through the same backend machinery as the rest of Sentence Transformers, so you get torch (default), onnx, and openvino, alongside half precision, Flash Attention, and torch.compile.

On GPU, fp16 with Flash Attention is the best configuration we measured, at 2.44x the throughput of fp32 with no measurable retrieval quality loss. Flash Attention helps multi-vector models more than most, because documents are only truncated and never padded to a shared length, so your batches have widely varying sequence lengths that unpadding can exploit:

Models with non-attend query expansion (attend=False, which covers the Stanford-NLP checkpoints like colbert-ir/colbertv2.0 and answerdotai/answerai-colbert-small-v1) reject Flash Attention at load time. Flash Attention strips attention_mask=0 positions, so the [MASK] expansion tokens that MaxSim scores would never receive an attention update. Use "sdpa" for those models.

On CPU, OpenVINO is your better bet where the architecture is supported, and int8 quantization buys a further speedup at a cost of about 0.4% accuracy. See Speeding up Inference for the full benchmark details, the export and quantization helpers, and a flowchart for picking a backend.

MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator runs the NanoBEIR suite of 13 small BEIR subsets with MaxSim scoring, and needs no data preparation on your side:

This also makes it easy to check the claim from the top of this post. lightonai/LateOn and lightonai/DenseOn were trained by LightOn on the same data with the same ModernBERT backbone and the same 149M parameters, differing only in whether they keep one vector per token or pool down to one per document. Running both over all 13 NanoBEIR datasets isolates what that choice buys:

Late interaction wins on 9 of the 13 datasets and on the mean, by roughly one NDCG point. The four it loses (ArguAna, FiQA2018, SCIDOCS, and SciFact) are the shape of the tradeoff you should expect, a real gain in retrieval quality at the same model size, paid for in index footprint, rather than a universal win on every dataset. The same pair scores 57.22 against 56.20 on the full 15-dataset BEIR, a comparable gap, so the margin is not an artifact of the small benchmark.

Alongside NanoBEIR, MultiVectorInformationRetrievalEvaluator, MultiVectorRerankingEvaluator, MultiVectorTripletEvaluator, and MultiVectorDistillationEvaluator cover the usual evaluation setups on your own data. They're documented in the Evaluation API Reference.

MultiVectorEncoder absorbs the modeling, inference, training, and evaluation of both libraries. Every PyLate checkpoint loads directly, and Supported Models lists the colpali-engine checkpoints along with the revision to pass where one is still needed. If you're migrating, these are the calls that change:

The difference worth knowing about is on bare (non-ColBERT) checkpoints, where PyLate's ColBERT("bert-base-uncased") applies the classic recipe by default while MultiVectorEncoder("bert-base-uncased") builds a plain stack, leaving the prefixes, query expansion, and skiplist as explicit choices. The training loss and evaluator equivalents, and the data-handling differences, are in the Migration Guide.

Save compatibility is one-way in every case. PyLate, Stanford-NLP ColBERT, and colpali-engine checkpoints all load into MultiVectorEncoder, but MultiVectorEncoder.save_pretrained output isn't loadable by any of them.

Models carrying the multi-vector and sentence-transformers tags on the Hub are the list that stays current, and we're working to get those tags onto every model that works. The tables below are what we test against directly, so treat them as a starting point rather than the full set. For text retrieval in particular, any PyLate or Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint loads whether or not it carries the tag yet.

Some entries need a small Sentence Transformers configuration added to their repository first, and several of those are still open pull requests at the time of writing. Where a revision is listed below, pass it until that pull request is merged, after which the plain model name is enough:

These load with their trained prefix tokens, query expansion, and punctuation skiplist recovered from the saved configuration.

The NanoBEIR column reports the mean NDCG@10 (higher is better) across the 13 NanoBEIR datasets, each a 50-query subsample of a BEIR dataset, as a fast proxy for English text retrieval quality. We used the MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator to compute the scores for the primarily-English models. A - means the model was not evaluated on it. Note that NanoBEIR is a small benchmark, and its scores aren't a substitute for evaluating on your own data, which is always the right way to pick a model.

ColPali-style models embed page images as documents and text as queries.

The NanoViDoRe column reports the mean NDCG@10 (higher is better) across NanoViDoRe v3, a compact visual document retrieval benchmark spanning 8 subsets (computer science, energy, finance in English and French, HR, industrial, pharmaceuticals, and physics). Like with NanoBEIR, NanoViDoRe is a small benchmark which shouldn't replace evaluation on your own data.

Most of these are LoRA adapter repositories, with the adapter applied directly onto its base at load time. Some also have a -merged sibling on the Hub (e.g. vidore/colpali-v1.3-merged) with the adapter already folded into the weights.

The three -hf entries are the transformers-native *ForRetrieval ports. They load without any configuration, but use more modeling from transformers and less from sentence_transformers. Generally, it's preferable to use the original models instead, as the ports score approximately the same.

Late interaction in Sentence Transformers rests on a lot of earlier work. Thanks to Omar Khattab and Matei Zaharia for ColBERT, which everything here descends from, and to the LightOn team (Antoine Chaffin, Raphael Sourty, Paulo Moura, and Amélie Chatelain) for PyLate and fast-plaid, which carried late interaction for years and shaped a good deal of the API described above.

Thanks to the ColPali team (Manuel Faysse, Hugues Sibille, Tony Wu, Bilel Omrani, Gautier Viaud, Céline Hudelot, and Pierre Colombo) for ColPali and colpali-engine, which brought late interaction to page images, and to Benjamin Clavié, Antoine Chaffin, and Griffin Adams for token pooling.

Thanks as well to the core MTEB team, Kenneth Enevoldsen and Roman Solomatin among many others, for MTEB and for the kind of hidden work that keeps information retrieval research running.

And thanks to everyone who trained and released the checkpoints in Supported Models. Without them this post would have had nothing to measure.

To learn how to train or finetune these models on your own data:

See the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers.

The guide's distinction between first-stage retrieval and late-interaction reranking is useful for comparing complete systems. A practical baseline is BM25 candidate generation followed by a reranker, measuring recall at the candidate cutoff as well as final nDCG and end-to-end cost. We evaluated that pattern on a small English corpus here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). We haven't benchmarked the multi-vector models in this guide, especially on long or visual documents, so a matched evaluation would be needed.

InfoQ Homepage News LinkedIn Replaces Argo CD with a Custom GitOps Engine for Kubernetes Deployments

Nov 12, 2026 4 min read

In a recent post, LinkedIn revealed it has replaced Argo CD with its own GitOps engine. This new system deploys applications across over 250 Kubernetes clusters. It supports more than 4,000 services and manages over 100,000 deployments each week. According to a post, deployment infrastructure failures fell from 925 to 63 despite a 3.7x increase in deployment volume. The median time to detect and conclude a failed deployment dropped from 16.1 to 2.45 minutes.

LinkedIn started with one Argo CD instance per cluster, a topology it chose because Argo CD already managed its cluster add-ons that way. Clusters run up to 5,000 nodes each. A central deployment orchestrator spawned an ephemeral pod per deployment, with Argo CD hidden behind it. The team lists seven problems that emerged at scale. Argo CD doesn't have an observedGeneration, so you can't link sync and health status to a specific deployment. LinkedIn created a Lua health check that uses a tracking annotation to address this. A Synced and Healthy application could also resolve to an unintended revision when stale repo-server cache entries were used.

Two of the issues were architectural. Argo CD maintains one watch per group-version-resource across Applications. LinkedIn’s clusters have low resource-type diversity. This means etcd churn from one app can slow syncs for all apps. In one test, sync took under 3 minutes on a cluster with 60,000 pods and over 10 minutes with more than 80,000. The second was server-side-apply PATCH. Kubernetes truncates managedFields once an object has had more than 10 distinct field managers, and the API server then forgets who owns a field. In LinkedIn's AI workloads, which run multiple containers per Pod, a container removed from a manifest could therefore survive on the live Pod. The team had pruning disabled because destructive operations in production require approval. The remaining problems were CRD schema changes that required controller restarts across the fleet. Some OutOfSync states did not reflect real drift. Error messages were buried in boilerplate.

LinkedIn evaluated Flux but found it shared the same controller paradigm, so it built the engine as a library. Each deployment runs in its pod, with no shared controller state. Updates use PUT for full replacements, not PATCH. They retry on resourceVersion conflicts with exponential backoff. A 3-way diff across the live object, the previously deployed manifest, and the newly rendered manifest detects drift, and genuine drift fails the deployment. The same pod then watches the object's status until it converges or times out, and the API server unwraps errors for the user. Objects missing from the rendered manifest become deletion candidates, subject to delete protection, and convergence logic for LinkedIn's CRDs is built in.

The comparison uses the same calendar month a year apart. The migration ran from July 2025 to April 2026, which makes May 2026 the first clean post-migration month. The infra failure count covers only failures caused by the deployment system and excludes drift errors, since the two systems define drift differently. LinkedIn states that the improvement isn't solely due to the new engine. The orchestrator's error classification and reliability also got better during this time. The median duration for successful deployments is similar for both systems. However, the mean and tail have improved. The team attributes this to a namespace-scoped informer cache.

The engine is internal, and no open-source release is mentioned. Argo CD remains in use at LinkedIn for cluster add-ons and system services. The team had also found that maintaining 200+ Argo CD instances made each upgrade a multi-week project.

Teams running Argo CD at scale can check two things without a rewrite. Count the field managers on long-lived objects, since managedFields truncation can leave orphaned containers that produce no error. Then check whether sync latency tracks total pod count on shared clusters, which points to watch contention. LinkedIn concludes that the build-or-extend decision relies on the operational model. They say that per-deployment isolation, not controller tuning, allows the system to scale with compute.

LinkedIn is not the only large operator to build deployment logic around Kubernetes rather than adopt a general-purpose GitOps controller. Uber’s Up platform assigns each deployment to a dedicated controller. This is the Uber Deployment Controller. It translates the intent into Kubernetes primitives and sends status updates. This helps the workflow move forward. Uber keeps a long-running controller, while LinkedIn runs one ephemeral pod per deployment with no shared controller state.

Airbnb went further back and built its own tooling years earlier. In a talk at QCon London 2019 on InfoQ, infrastructure engineer Melanie Cebula introduced kube-gen. This internal framework creates Kubernetes configuration from one versioned project file. It also includes a deploy tool that applies or replaces objects and restarts pods, so changes take effect right away. Airbnb's deploy tool also returns an atomic success or failure, and a container that restarts for 30 seconds at the start of a rollout counts as a failed deploy. Airbnb was then at roughly 125,000 production deploys a year.

#10068. Brit police watchdog says cops' use of facial recog risks wrongful arrests

New report calls for change, highlights hodgepodge governance and misunderstanding about tech’s limitations among officers

UK police forces must do more to prevent the wrongful arrests of people subjected to retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches, according to a Criminal Justice Inspectorate that holds deep concerns about the way in which the technology is used.

According to a report from His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS), there is a large gap in understanding among police forces and the National Crime Agency about how RFR should be used in responsible policing.

The inspectorate blamed "fragmented and underdeveloped" frameworks for governance and legislation.

It pointed to a lack of bespoke legislation to provide a uniform approach to police facial recognition use – and said existing laws have not kept pace with the technology. HMICFRS also said the rules governing each force's use of RFR are mismatched, and called for a statutory code to be included in the forthcoming Police Reform Bill to set nationwide standards.

Illustrating the breadth of misunderstanding across forces, the report noted that despite the message being routinely communicated by National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) reps, individual investigators "often" thought RFR results constituted evidence rather than intelligence.

In many cases, they are unaware that RFR results require further enquiries before enforcement action can be taken.

"We found that some investigators didn't always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches," the report stated. "In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action.

"Although some forces had strengthened their processes after such incidents, practice remained inconsistent."

Later in the report, the inspectorate described the findings as "deeply concerning."

Some of the excuses police staff offered included acute demands on response teams leading to reduced opportunities to carry out further enquiries before acting on RFR matches. In one force, managers were known to encourage officers to "progress investigations quickly" after getting a match on the RFR system.

However, the inspectorate clarified that just because an arrest is made, it does not necessarily mean it is wrongful, as investigators may need to rule out subjects from their inquiries.

The onus for taking action should also be placed on the police forces themselves, given that some lack formal procedures regarding how RFR enquiries should be carried out, the report noted.

The best forces had centralized facial recognition teams, which generally provided better governance and consistent processes.

Officials fear long-term misuse of RFR, and other forms of facial recognition, will erode public trust in the technology, which it insists remains generally high.

Surveys carried out in 2025 by the likes of the Ada Lovelace Institute and Alan Turing Institute, as well as the King's College London Policy Institute, showed a generally favorable view of facial recognition use in UK policing, with support ranging from 91 percent and 53 percent respectively.

Home Office figures released on Thursday to complement the report show similar positivity toward the technology among police officers, with only 4 percent reporting a negative experience.

The Register's comments section often paints a vastly different picture of public perception of facial recognition.

Kathryn Stone, his majesty's inspector at HMICFRS, said facial recognition has transformed policing, allowing officers to compare images in seconds, allowing them to solve crimes more quickly, but echoed the report's main concerns.

"Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment," she said.

"A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence."

As well as legislative and governance-related concerns, HMICFRS also noted in its report that officers' training around the use of RFR remains inconsistent, and if improvements were made, this would lead to more effective and lawful use of RFR across the UK.

Another major issue was police forces' failure to meet their image retention obligations. Forces were found too often to retain custody images taken of suspects on the Police National Database, against which many RFR queries are made.

Police guidance sets out the scenarios in which custody images can and cannot be retained, and the inspectorate found that forces have failed to delete images that should have been wiped.

The Police Reform Bill includes a provision to group custody images with the likes of DNA and fingerprints, bringing about more robust measures to ensure they are retained or deleted in line with legal requirements.

A Home Office review previously found in 2017 that introducing such a statutory framework was untenable. It concluded that police could not automate the deletion of these images, and doing so manually would be too time-consuming.

Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at Big Brother Watch, said UK police cannot be allowed to continue to use RFR when it risks wrongfully arresting individuals.

"The revelations that officers are treating facial recognition as bona fide evidence rather than a probability score is alarming," she said.

"This approach significantly increases the risk that more innocent people will have officers knock on their door to arrest them for crimes committed in towns they've never visited, as we've seen before.

"Worse still, police aren't even logging their use of retrospective facial recognition, meaning people could wrongfully become suspects in criminal investigations without any record of why they've been accused."

Chaggar called on the government to "urgently step in" and help the UK's police forces to sort out the new frameworks needed for effective RFR use. ®

#10067. Crackdown on UK medical record snooping after staff reported sneaking 300+ times this year

Watchdog wants assurances from 200 execs that employees aren't poking around patient files they have no business viewing

The ICO received and assessed more than 300 reports of medical record snooping between January and mid-October 2026. Staff were caught looking up people they knew, poking around patient files out of sheer curiosity, and sharing private information with people who had no business seeing it.

The figure covers reports submitted by healthcare organizations rather than confirmed breaches, and excludes cases still awaiting assessment.

ICO chief executive Paul Arnold wants health bosses to personally assure him that their organizations have safeguards in place to stop staff having a nose through records they aren't supposed to see.

"Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardize the vital trust people place in our health service," Arnold said.

In a three-page letter to chief executives, Arnold makes clear that simply trusting staff to behave themselves won't cut it. He wants to know who can access patient records, whether anyone is checking what they're looking at, and what happens when somebody gets caught snooping.

Health bosses are also expected to investigate suspected breaches without dragging their feet, work out whether patients need to be told, and take action against staff caught accessing records they shouldn't.

Executives have until November 27 to respond. Those who haven't reviewed their safeguards in the past six months, or aren't happy with what they find, have been given another three months to put their house in order.

The problem isn't necessarily that healthcare workers are hacking into systems, as many already have legitimate access to patient records as part of their jobs. The trouble starts when they use that access to look up someone they're not treating, whether it's a neighbor, an ex-partner, or somebody whose name has appeared in the news.

This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem. In July, NHS England warned employees that accessing records without a legitimate reason could cost them their jobs or even land them in prison.

That crackdown followed incidents involving staff accessing the medical records of victims of high-profile crimes, including the Nottingham attacks. NHS England also published guidance encouraging organizations to use access controls and audit systems to catch employees poking around where they shouldn't.

Some newer electronic patient record systems can even flag suspicious access in real time, although the NHS acknowledged that monitoring capabilities vary depending on the technology organizations have installed.

The scale of the problem has been troubling regulators for years. In July, the UK government told Parliament that 1,445 cases of inappropriate access had been reported to the ICO between 2019 and 2025.

And the consequences can go beyond getting the sack. The ICO has prosecuted 16 healthcare workers for snooping through patient records over the past decade, with unauthorized access to personal information potentially amounting to a criminal offense under the Data Protection Act 2018.

Arnold warned that the regulator could also take enforcement action against healthcare organizations whose protections aren't up to scratch.

"I've written to chief executives across the UK asking them to personally assure me that their safeguards work in practice. Where they don't, we expect organizations to put that right," he said.

With hundreds of reports already landing on the watchdog's desk this year, healthcare bosses now have a fortnight to explain how they're keeping staff out of records they have no business reading. ®

#10065. How Much Memory Does Your Agent Actually Need?

In our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and showed that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs. the whole set injected — drives both accuracy and cost. This post steps back to the question that comes before it: how much should you give it?

Equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance. It doesn't always work that way. When we scaled the evaluation to eight models — from a 30B dense model to frontier proprietary systems — one finding stood out:

Agentic memory is not a feature you switch on. It's a dose you calibrate to the model.

ALTK-Evolve lets an agent learn from its own past trajectories: distilling reusable guidelines and injecting them back at inference time, with no weight updates and no human annotation.

The right dose differs by model tier: strong models with headroom want the full guideline set, weaker models do best with a compact core plus per-task retrieval, and saturated models show no measurable gain.

Curated retrieval can be both the most accurate and the cheapest option: gpt-oss-120b gained +16.1pp task completion at only +5% tokens — and prompt caching keeps even the full guideline set affordable in production.

Not every model benefits from the same amount of memory. Across eight models spanning the capability spectrum, we saw three recurring patterns:

Strong models with headroom want the full guideline set — every guideline, including rare edge-case lessons. They have the capacity to absorb and apply all of it. DeepSeek-V3.2 (671B MoE) climbed +9.5 percentage points in task completion when given its full self-mined guideline set.

Smaller or weaker models get drowned by a large guideline set. For these, a tight, high-confidence core plus a handful of task-relevant guidelines retrieved per task works best. gpt-oss-120b (117B MoE) gained +16.1pp with this selective approach — while the full guideline set gained less and cost ~50% more tokens.

Already-saturated models show no measurable gain. We call this the saturated pattern — the label describes what we observed, not a proven cause. The model may already have been near its ceiling on these tasks, the guidelines may not have addressed its remaining failures, or it may not have applied the guidance effectively. GLM-5 (745B MoE) sat here in our runs.

What puts a model into one pattern rather than another isn't simply parameter count. Benchmark headroom, context-window size, architecture, guideline quality, and task distribution all appear to shape where a model lands, and separating those factors is ongoing work. The practical takeaway holds either way: the right dose of memory depends on the model, and we can calibrate it.

"Memory" here doesn't mean replaying a past transcript. It means a guideline set — strategies that worked, mistakes to avoid, and edge cases — distilled from the agent's own prior trajectories. The loop is straightforward:

The agent attempts tasks and produces trajectories.

ALTK-Evolve extracts behavioral guidelines from both its successful and unsuccessful runs.

It consolidates those guidelines into a reusable set.

At inference time, the agent receives either the full guideline set or a task-relevant selection of it.

No model weights are updated. The learning loop changes the guidance available to the agent, not the underlying model — which is exactly why it's cheap to adopt and portable across the eight models we tested.

We evaluated on AppWorld — 585 multi-step tasks (168 test_normal + 417 test_challenge) across 9 simulated apps (calendars, messaging, payments, and so on). Tasks are scored two ways: whether the agent fully completes each task (TGC — Task Goal Completion) and whether every variant of a scenario passes (SGC — Scenario Goal Completion, a stricter, all-or-nothing bar). Full definitions are in the appendix.

Because the confusing part of any memory study is what's actually in the context window, we define the configurations up front.

Both memory configurations draw from the same guideline set, mined once (via the loop above) from AppWorld's training split only. What changes between them is only how that one set is delivered — the full guideline set injects all of it every step, while curated retrieval delivers a selected subset — never how the guidelines were produced, and no test-split data ever goes into building it.

The number of guidelines a model mines depends on its own capability, so we report configurations by strategy — "full guideline set" vs. "curated retrieval" — rather than by raw counts, which aren't comparable across models.

Representative models from the eight-model sweep, measured by task completion (TGC) on test_normal:

Figure 1. Representative models in the three observed patterns. Bars show TGC on AppWorld test_normal for baseline vs. the best-memory configuration; the x-axis begins at 40% to make differences visible. TGC alone understates the larger SGC gains — see the SGC columns in the table below.

The figure plots TGC to keep it readable; the table adds the stricter SGC metric, where the gains are often larger:

Reading the SGC column, the stricter metric usually moves more than TGC — DeepSeek's SGC jumps +16.1pp against a +9.5pp TGC gain — because good guidelines especially help an agent clear every variant of a scenario, not just the average case. And the effect doesn't disappear at the top of the range: GPT-5.5 and Opus, both near the ceiling on TGC, still gain +7.2 and +7.1pp SGC respectively. Memory keeps paying off as long as a model has a remaining failure mode to target.

A practical concern: injecting a full guideline set inflates every ReAct step's input, because the guidelines are re-sent each turn. Here's what we observed:

Table 1. Average token use per task, accumulated across agent steps, measured against the no-memory baseline.

Curated retrieval keeps cost near baseline. For weaker models, where selection wins on accuracy, it also wins on cost — the best of both worlds (+16.1pp TGC at only +5% tokens for gpt-oss-120b). Better performance here does not require more inference cost.

Memory doesn't blow up the reasoning loop. DeepSeek runs about the same number of ReAct steps with memory as without (≈18–19 on average), so the added cost is input-token inflation, not longer trajectories.

The real efficiency lever in production is prompt caching: the static portion of the guideline set is identical across steps and can be cached, cutting effective cost substantially. Cache-aware prompt design — keeping the shared guideline-set prefix stable so it stays cacheable — is worth engineering for. We also hypothesize that context-window size plays a role: models with larger windows may absorb the full guideline set more effectively, while smaller-context models benefit more from retrieval that keeps injected content compact. We have not yet run controlled experiments isolating this factor.

The lesson isn't to give an agent everything it has learned. It's to give it the amount of experience it can actually use.

For weak models, that means a compact core plus a few task-specific lessons — which, conveniently, is also the cheapest option.

For strong models with headroom, it means preserving the full guideline set, kept affordable in production via prompt caching.

For saturated models, it means spending no extra context until their remaining failure modes are better understood.

The gains are real across the board — automatic, leakage-free, and requiring no human annotation — but only when the dose fits the model.

This is a starting point, not the finish line:

A learned selector. Our current retrieval ranks guidelines by cosine similarity, which we've shown doesn't perfectly predict which guidelines help a given task. A selector trained on outcome signal is the natural next step.

Memory for very weak models. Below a minimum capability baseline, self-distillation lacks signal. Teacher-distilled memory for very weak models is a separate problem we're exploring.

Beyond AppWorld. These results are validated on AppWorld — a rigorous multi-step benchmark, but a single one. Broader agent benchmarks and real-world deployments are in progress.

Isolating context window. As above, we want controlled experiments that separate context-window size from raw capability.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld tasks are graded by two metrics, both reported as percentages (higher is better):

TGC — Task Goal Completion. The share of individual tasks the agent completes fully and correctly. This is the headline "did it get the job done" number.

SGC — Scenario Goal Completion. A stricter, all-or-nothing metric. Each scenario bundles several variants of the same task (the same request with different data, phrasing, or edge conditions). SGC counts a scenario as passing only if the agent succeeds on every variant. It measures reliability — an agent that solves a task most of the time but fails on one variant scores on TGC but not on SGC.

Really interesting take on agentic memory. The idea that memory needs to be calibrated to the model rather than simply accumulated is especially useful for production systems. Selective retrieval also seems like a practical way to improve reliability without unnecessarily increasing context and inference costs. It makes a strong case for thoughtful custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions, where memory, performance, and cost all need to be designed together. https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-company
